cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Name and explain the criteria of statehood under international law. Which criterion is disputed, and what happens to an existing state that loses its effective government? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: A state exists when there is a permanent population, a defined territory and an effective, independent government (three-elements doctrine; Art 1 Montevideo Convention 1933); the fourth Montevideo criterion, capacity to enter into relations with other states, is disputed; an existing state does not disappear merely because its government collapses.
• Permanent population: a stable community bound to the state by nationality (rights of residence, return and political participation; duties such as taxes and military service). No minimum size (Nauru, Tuvalu, Liechtenstein).
• Defined territory: a stable core territory is enough; borders need not be fully delimited and border disputes do not prevent statehood (North Sea Continental Shelf 1969; Albania 1913; Israel 1949).
• Government: effective control over territory and population, plus independence – formally (no legal subordination to another state) and actually (not a puppet: Manchukuo 1932; Austro-German Customs Union AO, PCIJ 1931).
• Capacity to enter into relations with other states (Art 1(d)): disputed because it is rather a consequence of independent statehood than a separate condition; federal units or protectorates may have limited capacity without being states.
• Loss of effective government: presumption of continuity – the state survives (Somalia after 1991); extinction requires dissolution, merger or absorption.
• Contested additional requirement: an entity created in breach of ius cogens (unlawful force, denial of self-determination) is not accepted as a state (Southern Rhodesia 1965, TRNC 1983).
Memorise: Population · Territory · Government (effective + independent) · [capacity – disputed] – Montevideo 1933 Art 1 · continuity presumption · no statehood from a ius cogens breach.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: State Zorak invades its neighbour Norvania. In the occupied province, a 'Republic of East Norvania' proclaims independence; its administration runs the province, but all key decisions are taken by Zorak's officials and its budget is paid by Zorak. Meanwhile Norvania's central government has collapsed after years of civil war, and no authority controls more than the capital. Does Norvania still exist as a state? Is East Norvania a state? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Norvania continues to exist despite the collapse of its government; East Norvania is not a state – it lacks an independent government (a puppet of Zorak) and was created by an unlawful use of force, which triggers a duty of non-recognition.
• Criteria: permanent population, defined territory, effective and independent government (Art 1 Montevideo Convention 1933).
• Norvania: for an existing state the criteria are applied leniently – presumption of continuity; a temporary loss of effective government does not extinguish the state (Somalia after 1991). Its treaties, UN membership and territorial integrity remain.
• East Norvania: population, territory and a local administration exist, but no independent government – decisions and money come from Zorak, so it is a puppet entity (Manchukuo 1932, created by Japan; TRNC 1983, dependent on Turkey).
• Illegality: the entity results from Zorak's invasion (Art 2(4) UN Charter, ius cogens). It is not a state, and all states must not recognise it (Art 41(2) ARSIWA; SC Res 541 (1983) on the TRNC).
• Note: secession as such is not prohibited by international law (Kosovo AO 2010), but there is no general right to secede outside colonial or occupation contexts, and third states may not bring it about by force.
Memorise: existing state = continuity despite collapse · new state = effectiveness + independence · puppet ≠ state · created by force → non-recognition (Art 41(2) ARSIWA).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'An entity becomes a state only when it has been recognised by other states.' Give reasons. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – under the prevailing declaratory theory an entity is a state when it meets the factual criteria of statehood; recognition only acknowledges this, although it has important practical effects.
• Declaratory theory (prevailing, also the lecture's position): statehood depends on population, territory and effective government; recognition is a unilateral act confirming a fact (Art 3 Montevideo Convention: the political existence of a state is independent of recognition; Badinter Commission Opinion No. 1, 1991: the existence of a state is a question of fact, recognition is purely declaratory).
• Constitutive theory: recognition creates statehood. Objections: relativity (an entity would be a state for some and not for others), no central organ to decide, and unrecognised entities would stand outside the law – yet they are bound and protected by the prohibition of force.
• Practical relevance of recognition: evidence of statehood in doubtful cases (Kosovo), precondition for diplomatic relations and bilateral treaties, effects before domestic courts (standing, immunity); broad recognition consolidates a precarious entity, collective non-recognition isolates it.
Memorise: declaratory (fact) vs constitutive (creates) · Montevideo Art 3 · Badinter Op. 1 · recognition = evidence + relations, not creation.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Kardia, a province of State Mirena, declares independence. Mirena's army still controls two thirds of Kardia and heavy fighting continues. A week later (1) State Oskia sends Kardia a formal note recognising it 'as an independent and sovereign state'; (2) State Pelos concludes a bilateral trade treaty with Kardia; (3) State Quiros votes in the UN General Assembly in favour of admitting Kardia. Mirena protests. Assess the three acts. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Oskia's express recognition is premature and therefore an unlawful intervention in Mirena's internal affairs; Pelos's bilateral treaty amounts to implied (and equally premature) recognition; Quiros's vote is no recognition at all.
• Forms: recognition may be express (formal letter or note – e.g., Austria's letter of 25 April 1996 recognising the FRY) or implied through conduct that unequivocally shows the intention to treat the entity as a state: establishing diplomatic relations or concluding a bilateral treaty.
• Not implied recognition: voting for admission to an international organisation (a collective decision that can be taken by majority), participating with the entity in a multilateral treaty or conference, informal or trade contacts.
• Premature recognition: recognising a secessionist entity while the parent state is still effectively, and with prospects of success, fighting to keep control violates the prohibition of intervention and Mirena's territorial integrity (Biafra 1968, recognised by a few African states; criticism of the early recognition of Croatia 1991/92). Kardia controls only one third – no effective government yet.
• De iure recognition (full, final) vs de facto recognition (provisional, reserved, acknowledging effective control – e.g., the UK and the Soviet government 1921): Oskia gave de iure recognition.
• Consequence: the acts do not make Kardia a state (declaratory theory); Oskia and Pelos commit wrongful acts against Mirena (cessation, satisfaction).
Memorise: express vs implied (diplomatic relations, bilateral treaty) · NOT implied: IO vote, multilateral treaty · premature recognition = intervention · de facto (provisional) vs de iure (final).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: After invading neighbouring State Moravia, State Vortan formally annexes Moravia's province of Lissa. A referendum held under Vortan's military occupation shows 95% in favour of joining Vortan. Vortan asks State Tirania to recognise the new border and to conclude a fisheries treaty covering Lissa's coastal waters. May Tirania do so? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – conquest is no longer a valid title to territory, and all states are under a duty not to recognise as lawful a territorial acquisition resulting from the use of force; the occupation referendum does not cure this.
• Prohibition of force: Art 2(4) UN Charter, customary and peremptory; Friendly Relations Declaration 1970: no territorial acquisition resulting from the threat or use of force shall be recognised as legal (earlier: Stimson doctrine 1932).
• Duty of non-recognition: Art 41(2) ARSIWA – no state shall recognise as lawful a situation created by a serious breach of a peremptory norm, nor render aid or assistance in maintaining it. Practice: SC Res 662 (1990) – Iraq's annexation of Kuwait null and void; Namibia AO 1971; Wall AO 2004; GA Res 68/262 (2014) on Crimea.
• A referendum under foreign military occupation, without Moravia's consent, is no free exercise of self-determination and cannot legitimise the annexation.
• Consequence: Lissa remains Moravian territory; Tirania must not conclude treaties treating Vortan as sovereign over Lissa. Only acts benefiting the population (registration of births, deaths, marriages) may be given effect (Namibia AO, para 125).
Memorise: ex iniuria ius non oritur · Art 2(4) + FRD 1970 · Art 41(2) ARSIWA non-recognition · Kuwait (SC 662), Crimea (GA 68/262).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Which modes of acquiring territory are recognised in international law? Which of them is no longer valid today, and why? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Occupation of terra nullius, accretion, cession, prescription/acquiescence and adjudication (for new states: uti possidetis); conquest (annexation by force) is no longer a valid title because of the prohibition of the use of force.
• Occupation: only of terra nullius, by an effective, continuous and peaceful display of state authority with the intention to act as sovereign; discovery gives only an inchoate title (Island of Palmas 1928, Max Huber); for remote areas little display suffices (Eastern Greenland, PCIJ 1933; Clipperton 1931). Territory inhabited by organised tribes is not terra nullius (Western Sahara AO 1975); today hardly any is left (Antarctic claims frozen by the Antarctic Treaty 1959).
• Accretion: natural growth of land (e.g., a new volcanic island in the territorial sea).
• Cession: transfer by treaty (sale of Alaska 1867; Walvis Bay to Namibia 1994) – void if procured by force (Art 52 VCLT).
• Prescription / acquiescence: long, peaceful and public exercise of authority over another state's territory without protest (prescription contested as such, but acquiescence is accepted: Temple of Preah Vihear 1962; Pedra Branca 2008).
• Adjudication; for new states uti possidetis juris (Burkina Faso/Mali 1986).
• Conquest/annexation: invalid under Art 2(4) UN Charter and the Friendly Relations Declaration 1970; duty of non-recognition (Art 41(2) ARSIWA; Kuwait 1990, Crimea 2014).
• Intertemporal law: a title is judged by the law in force at the time of acquisition (Island of Palmas).
Memorise: Occupation (terra nullius + effectiveness, Palmas) · Accretion · Cession · Prescription/acquiescence · Adjudication/uti possidetis · NOT conquest (Art 2(4)).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Rachastan and Antrania gained independence 45 years ago from the same colonial power, which had administratively assigned the border region of Bethania to Antrania. Over 90% of Bethania's inhabitants are ethnic Rachastanis. Rachastan claims Bethania on ethnic and historical grounds and because its police have for decades patrolled several Bethanian villages. Antrania relies on the colonial boundary. Which state has the better title? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Antrania – under uti possidetis juris the colonial administrative boundary became the international frontier at independence; ethnic composition creates no title, and effectivités that contradict a legal title cannot override it.
• Uti possidetis juris: a new state inherits the administrative boundaries existing at the date of independence (critical date). Origin in 19th-century Latin America, adopted in Africa (OAU Cairo Resolution 1964), recognised as a general principle connected with decolonisation (Burkina Faso/Mali, ICJ Chamber 1986) and applied to the SFRY's internal borders (Badinter Opinion No. 3). Purpose: stability, preventing fratricidal border wars.
• Effectivités (actual exercise of state authority): if they match the title they only confirm it; if they contradict it, the title prevails; only where there is no title are they decisive (Burkina Faso/Mali, para 63; Cameroon v Nigeria 2002 – Bakassi). Rachastan's patrols contradict Antrania's title – irrelevant unless Antrania clearly acquiesced.
• Ethnic and historical ties are no legal title to territory (Western Sahara AO 1975). Self-determination of the Bethanians does not entitle them to join another state; it is exercised within existing borders (territorial integrity).
• Stability of boundaries: boundaries survive state succession (Art 11 VCST 1978) and cannot be terminated for a fundamental change of circumstances (Art 62(2)(a) VCLT).
• Result: Bethania belongs to Antrania; the dispute must be settled peacefully (Arts 2(3), 33 UN Charter), force is prohibited.
Memorise: uti possidetis juris (Burkina Faso/Mali 1986) · title > contradicting effectivités · ethnicity ≠ title (Western Sahara) · borders stable (Art 11 VCST, Art 62(2)(a) VCLT).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Stardust, a company from State Y, operates thousands of internet satellites orbiting at about 550 km. State X protests that the satellites flying over its territory violate its territorial sovereignty; State Y replies that since 1957 outer space has not been part of the territory of the state below. Who is right? Would it differ if Stardust flew a relay drone at 5 km altitude over State X? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: State Y is right as to the orbit – outer space is not subject to national sovereignty (custom since 1957, Art II Outer Space Treaty 1967) – but a drone at 5 km is in X's airspace, which is under X's complete and exclusive sovereignty.
• State territory: land, internal waters, territorial sea (up to 12 nm, UNCLOS) and the airspace above them; Art 1 Chicago Convention 1944: complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace – no right of innocent passage in the air.
• Outer space: after Sputnik (1957) no state protested against satellite overflights → practice + opinio iuris → customary freedom of outer space; codified in the Outer Space Treaty 1967 (free use, Art I; no national appropriation, Art II). No treaty boundary; orientation about 100 km – 550 km is clearly outer space.
• Private use is allowed, but Y bears international responsibility for its companies' space activities and must authorise and supervise them (Art VI OST).
• The drone at 5 km is in X's airspace → without X's consent a violation of X's sovereignty.
Memorise: airspace = sovereign (Chicago Art 1) · outer space = free, no appropriation (custom since 1957 + OST 1967 Arts I–II) · ~100 km · Art VI OST: responsibility for private actors.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Ms K, a national of State A working in State B, uses her laptop in State B to hack the power grid of State C, causing a blackout there, steals the credit-card data of nationals of State D and prints counterfeit banknotes of State E. She then travels to State F, which has no link to the facts. Which states may exercise criminal jurisdiction, and on what basis? May State C send police officers to State B to arrest her? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: B (territoriality), C (objective territoriality/effects and protective principle), A (active personality), D (passive personality) and E (protective principle) may prescribe and adjudicate; F has no basis because these are not crimes of universal jurisdiction; C may not enforce its jurisdiction on B's territory without B's consent.
• International law requires a sufficient link (genuine connection) between the regulating state and the conduct.
• Territoriality: B – the acts were committed there; objective territoriality / effects: C – the blackout occurred there (Lotus 1927: effects on the Turkish ship).
• Active personality: A – the offender is its national. Passive personality: D – the victims are its nationals (once contested, today accepted especially for serious offences).
• Protective principle: E – counterfeiting its currency threatens its vital interests; also C – attack on its critical infrastructure/security.
• Universality: only for crimes against the international community (piracy, genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture) – not for hacking or fraud → F has no basis; at most vicarious (representative) administration of criminal justice, prosecuting on behalf of a competent state where extradition is impossible.
• Prescriptive vs enforcement jurisdiction: several states may have concurrent prescriptive jurisdiction, but enforcement is strictly territorial – a state may not exercise its power in any form on another state's territory without a permissive rule (Lotus 1927). An arrest by C's police in B violates B's sovereignty (cf. Eichmann 1960, SC Res 138); C must request extradition or mutual legal assistance.
Memorise: Territory (+effects) · Active · Passive · Protective · Universal · Vicarious · prescribe ≠ enforce (Lotus: enforcement only on own territory).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'According to the Lotus case, a state may apply its criminal law to any conduct abroad unless a prohibitive rule exists, and it may also enforce its law anywhere.' (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Only the first half reflects Lotus (and is criticised today); the second half is wrong – Lotus held that enforcement jurisdiction is strictly territorial.
• Facts: 1926 high-seas collision between the French Lotus and the Turkish Boz-Kourt; Turkey prosecuted the French officer of the watch. PCIJ 1927 (casting vote): no rule prohibited Turkey; effects on a Turkish ship counted like effects on Turkish territory.
• Holdings: enforcement – a state may not exercise its power in any form on another state's territory without a permissive rule; prescription – wide discretion, limited only by prohibitive rules.
• Today a recognised basis and a genuine link are required; for collisions the result was reversed by treaty (Art 97 UNCLOS: only the flag state or the state of nationality).
Memorise: Lotus 1927 · enforcement = territorial · prescription = free unless prohibited (criticised) · Art 97 UNCLOS reversed the collision rule.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: The multiethnic state of Bellivonia is to be divided into two parts, which all political forces agree on: the larger state Bellistan (more than 80% of Bellivonia's territory) and the smaller state Livonia. Bellistan's scholars claim that Bellistan continues the legal identity of Bellivonia under a new name as the 'rump state' and only Livonia is a new state; Livonia argues that Bellivonia has ceased to exist and both are successor states. What does 'state succession' mean? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: State succession is the replacement of one state by another in the responsibility for the international relations of a territory (Art 2(1)(b) VCST 1978; Art 2(1)(a) VCSSPAD 1983).
• It is a change of sovereignty over territory – not a change of government, name or constitution, which leaves the state's identity untouched (continuity).
• The question is which rights and obligations of the predecessor (treaties, property, archives, debts, nationality, IO membership) pass to the successor; only successions in conformity with international law are covered (Art 6 VCST) – annexation by force is none.
• Trap: a state that continues the predecessor's identity (Bellistan's claim) is no successor; succession then concerns only the new state (Livonia).
Memorise: replacement of one state by another in responsibility for the international relations of territory · Art 2(1)(b) VCST · ≠ change of government · Art 6: only lawful successions.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: The multiethnic state of Bellivonia is to be divided into two parts, which all political forces agree on: the larger state Bellistan (more than 80% of Bellivonia's territory) and the smaller state Livonia. Bellistan's scholars claim that Bellistan continues the legal identity of Bellivonia under a new name as the 'rump state' and only Livonia is a new state; Livonia argues that Bellivonia has ceased to exist and both are successor states. How should the division of Bellivonia be classified under international law if one follows Bellistan's view? What type of state succession does Livonia's view represent? Briefly justify. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: On Bellistan's view there is continuity (identity) – Bellistan is Bellivonia under a new name as the rump state – combined with the secession/separation of Livonia as the only new state; Livonia's view describes a dismembratio (dissolution): Bellivonia has ceased to exist and two new successor states have emerged.
• Bellistan's view: the predecessor survives with reduced territory; a change of name and loss of territory do not affect identity. Bellistan is not a successor but the same subject of international law; only Livonia separated → one case of succession (secession/separation), Livonia = new state succeeding for its territory. Precedents: Russia continuing the USSR 1991; Serbia continuing Serbia and Montenegro 2006; Sudan after South Sudan 2011; Pakistan after Bangladesh 1971.
• Consequences: Bellistan keeps Bellivonia's treaties (Art 35 VCST), its UN membership and embassies; property and debts are shared with Livonia by agreement or in equitable proportions (Arts 17, 40 VCSSPAD); Livonia must apply for membership in IOs and succeeds to treaties under Art 34 VCST.
• Livonia's view: dismembratio – the predecessor disappears and two new states emerge on an equal footing, none continuing its identity (Czechoslovakia 1 Jan 1993 → Czech Republic + Slovakia; SFRY per Badinter Opinions 8 and 10, the FRY's continuity claim being rejected – GA Res 47/1 (1992), admission as a new member in 2000).
• Consequences: both must apply for UN membership; property, archives and debts are divided equitably (Arts 18, 31, 41 VCSSPAD); treaties continue for each successor (Art 34 VCST).
• Which view prevails depends on the criteria of classification (territory, population, capital, agreement, recognition).
Memorise: Bellistan = continuity (rump state) + secession of Livonia · Livonia = dismembratio, 2 successors · models: Russia/USSR vs Czechoslovakia/SFRY.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: The multiethnic state of Bellivonia is to be divided into two parts, which all political forces agree on: the larger state Bellistan (more than 80% of Bellivonia's territory) and the smaller state Livonia. Bellistan's scholars claim that Bellistan continues the legal identity of Bellivonia under a new name as the 'rump state' and only Livonia is a new state; Livonia argues that Bellivonia has ceased to exist and both are successor states. Besides the self-assessment of the states concerned, which objective or subjective criteria are relevant for classifying a case of state succession? Name at least two. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Objective criteria – the share of territory and population retained and the retention of the capital and central state institutions; subjective/external criteria – agreement between the states concerned and recognition/acceptance by third states and international organisations, especially continued UN membership.
• Objective: Bellistan holds >80% of the territory – a strong indicator of continuity (Russia kept about three quarters of the USSR's territory and half its population); capital, central organs, armed forces, diplomatic network.
• Subjective: the entity's own claim (necessary, not sufficient); agreement (CIS decision of 21 Dec 1991 supporting Russia's continuation of the USSR's UN seat); reaction of third states and the UN (Russia accepted; the FRY's claim rejected, GA Res 47/1 (1992)).
• Here Livonia disagrees, so the attitude of third states and the UN will be decisive.
Memorise: territory + population + capital/institutions (objective) · own claim + agreement + recognition/UN membership (subjective).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: The multiethnic state of Bellivonia is to be divided into two parts, which all political forces agree on: the larger state Bellistan (more than 80% of Bellivonia's territory) and the smaller state Livonia. Bellistan's scholars claim that Bellistan continues the legal identity of Bellivonia under a new name as the 'rump state' and only Livonia is a new state; Livonia argues that Bellivonia has ceased to exist and both are successor states. Bellistan and Livonia agree that the citizens of Bellivonia shall have dual citizenship of both states. Which state may exercise diplomatic protection for such a dual national against a third country? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Each state of nationality – Bellistan or Livonia – may exercise diplomatic protection against a third state, alone or jointly (Art 6 ILC Draft Articles on Diplomatic Protection 2006); no effective or predominant nationality test applies vis-à-vis third states.
• Nationality acquired through state succession is a recognised mode (Art 4 DADP); the third state cannot object that it is not the 'effective' nationality, unless it was acquired abusively.
• Contrast: against one of the two states of nationality (e.g., Livonia claiming against Bellistan) Art 7 applies – only if the claimant's nationality is predominant at the date of injury and at the official presentation of the claim.
• Trap: 'the state with the more genuine link' is correct only between the two national states, not towards third states.
Memorise: vs third state → Art 6: each or jointly · vs other national state → Art 7: predominant nationality (both dates).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: The multiethnic state of Bellivonia is to be divided into two parts, which all political forces agree on: the larger state Bellistan (more than 80% of Bellivonia's territory) and the smaller state Livonia. Bellistan's scholars claim that Bellistan continues the legal identity of Bellivonia under a new name as the 'rump state' and only Livonia is a new state; Livonia argues that Bellivonia has ceased to exist and both are successor states. Livonia declares that, as an equal successor, it automatically holds a seat in the UN and in all organisations of which Bellivonia was a member, and that it is party to all of Bellivonia's multilateral treaties. Bellistan claims that it alone continues Bellivonia's memberships. Assess. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Membership in international organisations does not pass by succession – a new state must be admitted under the constituent treaty (Art 4 UN Charter); only a continuing state keeps the predecessor's seat. Ordinary treaties are different: under Art 34 VCST they continue for each successor.
• Membership is governed by the constituent instrument, which makes admission subject to a decision (UN: Art 4 – recommendation of the Security Council and a two-thirds decision of the General Assembly); Art 4 VCST expressly leaves the rules on acquisition of membership unaffected.
• Practice: Czech Republic and Slovakia admitted anew (19 Jan 1993); the FRY had to apply (GA Res 47/1 (1992)), admitted 1 Nov 2000; South Sudan admitted 14 July 2011. A continuing state keeps its seat (Russia for the USSR, including the permanent Security Council seat; Serbia 2006). If Livonia's dissolution view prevailed, both would have to apply.
• Multilateral treaties: those in force for the whole territory continue for each successor (Art 34 VCST) unless otherwise agreed or incompatible; in practice confirmed by notifications of succession to the depositary.
Memorise: IO membership ≠ automatic (Art 4 UN Charter; Art 4 VCST) · continuing state keeps the seat (Russia) · new states apply (CZ/SK 1993, FRY 2000, South Sudan 2011).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Explain the different forms of state succession and give examples. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The forms differ in whether the predecessor survives and whether a new state emerges: transfer (cession) of part of a territory, secession/separation, dismembratio (dissolution), merger/fusion, incorporation (absorption) and – in decolonisation – newly independent states.
• Transfer/cession of part of a territory: territory passes from one existing state to another, both continue (Alaska 1867 from Russia to the USA; Walvis Bay 1994 from South Africa to Namibia; Hong Kong 1997 from the UK to China). Treaties: moving treaty frontiers (Art 15 VCST).
• Secession/separation: a part breaks away and forms a new state; the predecessor continues with reduced territory (Bangladesh from Pakistan 1971; Eritrea from Ethiopia 1993; Montenegro from Serbia and Montenegro 2006; South Sudan from Sudan 2011; the Soviet republics 1991 with Russia as continuing state). Secession usually denotes a break-away against the parent state's will, separation one by agreement.
• Dismembratio/dissolution: the predecessor ceases to exist and two or more new successor states emerge (Austria-Hungary 1918; SFRY 1991–92; Czechoslovakia 1993).
• Merger/fusion: two or more states unite into a new state, all predecessors disappear (Tanganyika + Zanzibar → Tanzania 1964; North and South Yemen → Republic of Yemen 1990).
• Incorporation/absorption: a state joins another existing state, which continues (GDR into the FRG, 3 Oct 1990, Art 23 Basic Law). Annexation by force is unlawful and no valid succession (Austria 1938 – restored 1945; Kuwait 1990; Crimea 2014).
• Newly independent states (Art 2(1)(f), Art 16 VCST): former dependent territories becoming independent in decolonisation (e.g., Ghana 1957, Algeria 1962).
• Distinguish continuity: a change of name, government or size of territory creates no new state.
Memorise: predecessor survives? YES → cession, secession/separation, incorporation (absorbing state) · NO → dismembratio, merger · + newly independent states · Alaska · South Sudan · CS/SFRY · Yemen · GDR→FRG.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Name the sources of law applicable to state succession in respect of treaties and outline the different principles in that respect. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The 1978 Vienna Convention on Succession of States in respect of Treaties (VCST, in force 1996, few parties), customary international law and case-specific instruments (devolution agreements, unilateral declarations, notifications of succession); the principles range from universal succession through the clean slate to moving treaty frontiers, with territorial treaties surviving in every case.
• Sources: VCST 1978 – binding only on its parties (about two dozen) and for successions after its entry into force (Art 7); partly codification (Arts 11–12), partly progressive development (Art 34). Custom decides most cases. Devolution agreements do not by themselves bind third states (Art 8); a unilateral declaration alone does not make the successor a party (Art 9); IO constituent treaties follow membership rules (Art 4).
• Theories: universal succession (all treaties pass), clean slate/tabula rasa (none pass), pick and choose.
• Moving treaty frontiers (Art 15): on transfer of territory the predecessor's treaties cease to apply there and the acquiring state's treaties extend to it.
• Clean slate (Art 16): a newly independent state is not bound, but may join multilateral treaties by notification of succession (Art 17); bilateral treaties only by agreement or conduct (Art 24).
• Uniting of states (Art 31): each predecessor's treaties continue for its former territory.
• Separation and dissolution (Art 34): ipso iure continuity for each successor; a continuing state keeps its treaties (Art 35). Exceptions: agreement, incompatibility with object and purpose, radical change of conditions.
• Always: boundaries and boundary regimes (Art 11) and other territorial regimes – transit, river navigation, demilitarisation (Art 12) – survive (customary: Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997); highly political treaties (alliances, neutrality) do not pass.
Memorise: VCST 1978 + custom + agreements/declarations · Art 15 moving frontiers · Art 16 clean slate · Art 31 unification · Art 34 continuity · Arts 11–12 borders/territorial regimes survive · political treaties lapse.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: State P has concluded (i) a bilateral investment treaty with State Z, (ii) a boundary treaty with its neighbour, (iii) a military alliance and (iv) the ICCPR. What happens to these treaties if (a) region R secedes and P continues, (b) P dissolves into two new states Q and R, (c) P's colony C becomes independent (as far as the treaties applied to C), (d) P absorbs neighbouring State S? From which legal sources do the rules derive? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The boundary treaty survives in every case and the alliance never passes; for the other treaties it depends on the form – continuity for separation and dissolution (Art 34 VCST), clean slate for the colony (Art 16), and extension of the absorbing state's treaties in the case of absorption (moving treaty frontiers in practice).
• Sources: VCST 1978 (few parties), customary law, devolution agreements and unilateral declarations/notifications.
• (a) Secession: P keeps all its treaties (Art 35). R: treaties in force for its territory (BIT, ICCPR) continue under Art 34 unless otherwise agreed or incompatible – customary status uncertain, so practice uses notifications and confirmations. Boundary treaty binds R (Art 11). Alliance: highly political – does not pass to R.
• (b) Dissolution: P disappears; for Q and R as for R in (a) – e.g., the Czech Republic and Slovakia declared themselves bound by Czechoslovak treaties from 1 Jan 1993. The alliance lapses.
• (c) Newly independent C: clean slate (Art 16) – not bound by the BIT or the alliance; may join the ICCPR by notification of succession (Art 17); bilateral treaties only by agreement (Art 24). Boundary treaty binds (Art 11; uti possidetis). The UN Human Rights Committee (General Comment 26, 1997) argues that ICCPR protection devolves with the territory – contested.
• (d) Absorption: S disappears. VCST Art 31 would keep S's treaties in force for S's former territory, but German practice in 1990 applied moving treaty frontiers: the FRG's treaties extended to the former GDR, the GDR's treaties were reviewed with the other parties (Unification Treaty Arts 11–12). S's boundary treaties remain.
Memorise: borders always survive (Art 11) · alliances never · separation/dissolution = continuity (Art 34) · colonies = clean slate (Art 16, notification Art 17) · absorption = moving frontiers in practice (Germany 1990), Art 31 on paper.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Classify the following events under the law of state succession and state briefly who continued or succeeded whom: (a) the end of the USSR in December 1991 (including the Baltic states); (b) the break-up of the SFRY 1991–92; (c) the division of Czechoslovakia on 1 January 1993; (d) German unification on 3 October 1990; (e) the independence of South Sudan (2011) and of Montenegro (2006). (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) separation of the republics with Russia as continuing state, the Baltic states restoring their pre-1940 statehood; (b) dismembratio – the FRY's continuity claim was rejected; (c) agreed dismembratio; (d) incorporation of the GDR into the continuing FRG; (e) secession/separation with Sudan and Serbia continuing.
• (a) USSR: the Alma-Ata Declaration (21 Dec 1991) said the USSR 'ceases to exist', but the CIS states supported Russia continuing its UN membership including the permanent Security Council seat, and third states accepted it → Russia continuing state, the other republics successor states (Russia took over the foreign debt and assets). The Baltic states restored the statehood illegally ended in 1940 – no succession to the USSR.
• (b) SFRY: Badinter Opinions 1 (process of dissolution), 8 (dissolution complete), 10 (the FRY is a new state); GA Res 47/1 (1992) denied the FRY automatic continuation; admitted as a new member in 2000; assets divided by the Agreement on Succession Issues (Vienna 2001).
• (c) Czechoslovakia: dissolution by constitutional act of 25 Nov 1992; neither continues; both admitted to the UN on 19 Jan 1993; treaties continued for both.
• (d) Germany: the GDR acceded to the FRG under Art 23 Basic Law → incorporation; the FRG continued its identity and UN seat; Unification Treaty Arts 11–12 (FRG treaties extended, GDR treaties reviewed).
• (e) South Sudan: agreed secession (2005 peace agreement, 2011 referendum); Sudan continues; UN member 14 July 2011. Montenegro: separation after the 2006 referendum; Serbia continues the State Union's personality and UN seat.
Memorise: USSR → Russia continuator (+ Baltics restored) · SFRY = dismembratio (Badinter 8, 10; FRY new 2000) · CS = agreed dismembratio · GDR → FRG incorporation · South Sudan / Montenegro = secession with continuing state.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Is there succession with regard to state property (assets) and to state responsibility? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes for state property, archives and debts, which pass according to territoriality and equity (1983 Vienna Convention, not in force; custom; agreements); for state responsibility the traditional rule is no succession, but modern practice admits it in certain cases, especially by agreement or after dissolution.
• Property passes without compensation (Art 11 VCSSPAD): immovables to the state where they lie, movables connected with the territory to that successor, the rest in equitable proportions (Arts 17–18); archives follow the territory; debts pass in equitable proportions after separation or dissolution (Arts 40–41); agreements prevail (SFRY Agreement on Succession Issues 2001).
• Responsibility: traditionally personal to the wrongdoer – it stays with a continuing state and lapses with an extinct one (ARSIWA covers only insurgents founding a new state, Art 10(2)). Modern trend: Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997 – Slovakia liable for, and entitled to compensation for, Czechoslovakia's conduct via the special agreement; Institut de Droit International, Tallinn 2015; ILC topic since 2017.
Memorise: property/archives/debts = pass (territory + equity; VCSSPAD 1983 not in force) · responsibility = traditionally no succession, today by agreement (Gabčíkovo).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: State Karstan dissolves into North and South Karstan, which cannot agree on the distribution of: (1) a World Bank loan used for a dam in the South; (2) bonds sold to foreign banks to finance a military campaign to suppress the population of the South; (3) Karstan's central bank gold held in Zurich; (4) the land-registry archives of the South, kept in the capital, which is now in the North. How should they be distributed? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Absent agreement: the dam loan goes mainly to the South (localised debt, equitable proportion); the war bonds are arguably 'odious debts' that do not bind the South; the gold is divided in equitable proportions; the South's archives pass to the South.
• Rules: 1983 Vienna Convention on Succession of States in respect of State Property, Archives and Debts (VCSSPAD) – not in force, partly customary; priority of agreement between the successors (SFRY Agreement on Succession Issues 2001).
• Debts (Art 41, dissolution): pass to the successors in equitable proportions, taking into account the property, rights and interests passing to them; 'state debt' in the Convention = financial obligation towards another state, an IO or another subject of international law (Art 33) – the World Bank loan qualifies. A debt tied to a project on one successor's territory is allocated mainly to that successor (benefit).
• Odious debts (doctrine, A. Sack 1927): debts contracted by a regime for purposes contrary to the interests of the population, such as war against or subjugation of that population, with the creditors' knowledge, do not pass to the successor (e.g., US refusal of Cuba's Spanish debts 1898). Customary status uncertain; the VCSSPAD does not codify it.
• Property (Art 18): immovable property passes to the state where it lies; other movable property (gold, reserves) in equitable proportions.
• Archives (Art 31): archives relating to a successor's territory pass to it; others shared equitably or by copies.
Memorise: agreement first · debts = equitable proportion (Art 41), localised debts to the beneficiary · odious debts not transferred (contested) · property: immovable by location, movable equitably · archives follow territory.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Former colony Lumaria became independent in 1962. In 2025 its new government declares that, as a newly independent state, it is not bound by (1) a 1905 treaty between the former colonial power and State Pelagon fixing their common boundary, (2) a 1910 treaty granting Pelagon a right of transit through Lumaria to the sea, and (3) a 1950 military alliance concluded by the colonial power. Assess. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Lumaria is right about the alliance (clean slate for newly independent states, Art 16 VCST) but bound by the boundary (Art 11) and the transit regime (Art 12) – territorial treaties survive every form of succession.
• Clean slate (Art 16 VCST): a newly independent state is not bound to maintain in force a treaty merely because it was in force for its territory; alliances are highly political and never pass.
• Art 11: a succession does not as such affect a boundary established by a treaty, nor the boundary regime. Art 12: obligations and rights relating to the use of territory established by treaty for the benefit of a foreign territory (transit, navigation, water use) are not affected – customary law (Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997, para 123). Exception: foreign military bases (Art 12(3)).
• Supported by uti possidetis juris (Burkina Faso/Mali 1986; OAU Cairo Resolution 1964) and the permanence of boundaries: a boundary established by treaty achieves a permanence the treaty itself may lack (Libya/Chad 1994); no termination of a boundary treaty for fundamental change of circumstances (Art 62(2)(a) VCLT).
• In addition, 63 years of conduct accepting the boundary would amount to acquiescence.
Memorise: newly independent = clean slate (Art 16) BUT borders (Art 11) + territorial regimes (Art 12) survive · Libya/Chad: boundary permanence · Art 62(2)(a) VCLT.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: State Varda dissolves into Nordvarda and Sudvarda. Nordvarda grants its nationality only to persons of Nordvardan ethnicity; Sudvarda grants its nationality only to residents of its own territory. As a result, 30,000 ethnic Sudvardans who have lived in Nordvarda for generations become stateless. Is this consistent with international law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Probably not – although each state determines its nationals, international law on succession requires states to prevent statelessness, presumes that habitual residents acquire the successor's nationality and prohibits discrimination.
• Principle: nationality is in principle a domestic matter, but within the limits set by international law (Nationality Decrees in Tunis and Morocco, PCIJ 1923). Acquisition through state succession is a recognised mode (Art 4 DADP).
• ILC Articles on Nationality of Natural Persons in relation to the Succession of States (1999, annexed to GA Res 55/153 (2000)): right to the nationality of at least one successor (Art 1); duty to prevent statelessness (Art 4); presumption that habitual residents acquire the nationality of the successor where they live (Art 5); right of option (Art 11); no discrimination (Art 15) and no arbitrary decisions (Art 16).
• Treaties: 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness (Art 10); European Convention on Nationality 1997; prohibition of racial discrimination (ICERD).
• Application: Nordvarda's ethnic criterion is discriminatory and ignores habitual residence; both successors share the duty to avoid statelessness – Nordvarda should grant nationality or at least an option.
Memorise: state decides nationality BUT: avoid statelessness · habitual-residence presumption · right of option · non-discrimination (ILC 1999 Articles, GA Res 55/153).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Journalist Joelle, preparing a report for a TV station based in State B, was arrested during a climate protest in State A and detained for five days; she was not allowed to contact her lawyer or family and could not apply for release. On release she was told that her valuable equipment (camera, recording devices, laptop) had been destroyed 'for security reasons'. Her attempts to obtain compensation for the equipment and the arrest before the courts of State A failed. Joelle acquired A's citizenship by birth and became a citizen of State B by naturalisation 10 years ago; she expects support from her 'new' home State B. What does Joelle mean by 'support' from State B? Briefly explain the prerequisites for this kind of support. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: She means diplomatic protection – State B invoking A's international responsibility for the injury to its national; it requires an internationally wrongful act of A injuring Joelle, B's nationality at the relevant times (and, against A, predominance of that nationality), exhaustion of local remedies, and B's discretionary decision to take up the claim.
• Concept: invocation by a state, through diplomatic action or other means of peaceful settlement, of the responsibility of another state for an injury caused by an internationally wrongful act to its natural or legal national (Art 1 ILC Draft Articles on Diplomatic Protection 2006, DADP); the state asserts its own right (Mavrommatis, PCIJ 1924). Means: protest, negotiation, arbitration, the ICJ if jurisdiction exists – never force.
• (1) Internationally wrongful act of A: conduct of its security authorities (Art 4 ARSIWA) – arbitrary, incommunicado detention without a possibility to challenge it (Art 9 ICCPR), no access to lawyer and family, interference with press freedom and assembly (Arts 19, 21 ICCPR), destruction of property without compensation.
• (2) Nationality of claims: naturalisation is a recognised mode (Art 4 DADP); continuous nationality from the injury to the official presentation of the claim (Art 5) – met, she was naturalised 10 years earlier. As she is also A's national, B's nationality must be predominant (Art 7) – see b).
• (3) Exhaustion of local remedies (Art 14; Interhandel 1959): A must have the chance to redress the wrong itself – her claims failed in A's courts; met if she used all available instances, otherwise an Art 15 exception is needed.
• (4) Espousal: B decides whether, how and how long to protect her (Barcelona Traction 1970) – see c).
• Aim: cessation and full reparation – compensation for detention and equipment, satisfaction (Arts 31–37 ARSIWA), paid to B.
Memorise: DP = state's own right (Mavrommatis, Art 1 DADP) · wrongful act + nationality (continuous; predominant vs other national state) + local remedies (Arts 14–15) + discretion (Barcelona Traction).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Journalist Joelle, preparing a report for a TV station based in State B, was arrested during a climate protest in State A and detained for five days; she was not allowed to contact her lawyer or family and could not apply for release. On release she was told that her valuable equipment (camera, recording devices, laptop) had been destroyed 'for security reasons'. Her attempts to obtain compensation for the equipment and the arrest before the courts of State A failed. Joelle acquired A's citizenship by birth and became a citizen of State B by naturalisation 10 years ago; she expects support from her 'new' home State B. Does Joelle's dual citizenship present an obstacle? She explains that although she still has a distant uncle in State A whom she visits now and then, she moved her professional environment and permanent residence to State B about 15 years ago, where she now lives with her husband and son. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – against another state of nationality, B may protect her only if B's nationality is predominant both at the date of injury and at the official presentation of the claim (Art 7 DADP); on these facts B's nationality clearly predominates.
• Traditional rule: no diplomatic protection against a state whose nationality the person also possesses (Art 4 Hague Convention on Nationality 1930 – equality of the nationalities).
• Modern rule: dominant/effective nationality (Mergé case, Italian–US Conciliation Commission 1955; Iran–US Claims Tribunal, Case A/18, 1984), codified in Art 7 DADP.
• Relevant factors: habitual residence, family, professional life, centre of interests, taxes, political participation, language, which passport is used.
• Application: 15 years' permanent residence, work, husband and son in B versus a distant uncle and occasional visits to A → B's nationality is predominant at the date of injury and when the claim is presented → B may protect Joelle against A.
• Variant: had a third State C arrested her, dual nationality would be no obstacle at all – any state of nationality (A or B, or both jointly) may protect her without an effectiveness test (Art 6 DADP).
Memorise: vs other national state → Art 7: predominant nationality at injury AND at presentation (Mergé 1955, A/18) · vs third state → Art 6: any state · factors: residence, family, work, centre of life.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Journalist Joelle, preparing a report for a TV station based in State B, was arrested during a climate protest in State A and detained for five days; she was not allowed to contact her lawyer or family and could not apply for release. On release she was told that her valuable equipment (camera, recording devices, laptop) had been destroyed 'for security reasons'. Her attempts to obtain compensation for the equipment and the arrest before the courts of State A failed. Joelle acquired A's citizenship by birth and became a citizen of State B by naturalisation 10 years ago; she expects support from her 'new' home State B. Does Joelle have a right under international law to State B's support? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – diplomatic protection is a discretionary right of the state, not a right of the individual under international law; at most domestic (constitutional) law may give her a claim that her request be duly considered.
• Barcelona Traction (ICJ 1970): the state is the sole judge whether, to what extent and for how long it grants protection, and may decide on political grounds; B may also settle or waive the claim, and compensation is paid to B.
• Art 19 DADP (recommended practice, not binding): B should give due consideration to protection where significant injury occurred, take her views into account and transfer the compensation obtained.
• Domestic law may add a duty to consider her request within a wide discretion (German Federal Constitutional Court, Hess 1980; UK Court of Appeal, Abbasi 2002). Her own avenue: human rights complaints against A, where A has accepted them.
Memorise: DP = discretion of the state (Barcelona Traction) · no individual right in international law · Art 19 DADP 'should' (soft) · domestic law may add a right to consideration.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Variant of a diplomatic-protection case: Joelle, a national of State A by birth who lives and works in State A, bought the nationality of State B under a citizenship-by-investment programme three months ago without ever living there. During a protest in State A she is arbitrarily detained and her equipment destroyed; she has exhausted A's remedies. (i) Can B protect her against A? (ii) Would it differ if the detention had taken place in a third State C? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (i) No – against A, B's nationality is not predominant (Art 7 DADP); (ii) against a third state both A and B are in principle entitled (Art 6), but C could object under Nottebohm that B's nationality lacks any genuine link – a contested point, whereas A's protection would be unproblematic.
• (i) Art 7: against another state of nationality only if the claimant's nationality is predominant at the date of injury and at presentation – here residence, work and life are all in A.
• (ii) Nottebohm (Liechtenstein v Guatemala, ICJ 1955): nationality is a legal bond based on a social fact of attachment, a genuine connection of existence, interests and sentiments; a nationality lacking it was not opposable to Guatemala.
• The ILC (commentary to Art 4 DADP) confined Nottebohm to its facts – no general genuine-link test – but the nationality must not be acquired abusively or contrary to international law; a purchased nationality without residence is the modern Nottebohm scenario (cf. CJEU, Commission v Malta, 2025, under EU law).
• Continuity (Art 5) is met in both scenarios, as she held B's nationality before the injury.
Memorise: vs own other national state → Art 7 predominance fails · vs third state → Art 6, but Nottebohm genuine-link objection (ILC: only abuse) · birth nationality (A) safe.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Variant of a diplomatic-protection case: Joelle, a national of State B, is detained in State A and her equipment destroyed. She did not go to A's courts at all: A's statute excludes any compensation claim against the security forces, and A's Supreme Court has rejected 40 identical claims by journalists. B immediately files an application against A before the ICJ; A objects that local remedies were not exhausted. Would it differ if she had sued and the case had been pending at first instance for 12 years? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: A's objection fails – where a statutory bar and consistent supreme-court case law leave no reasonable possibility of effective redress, exhaustion is not required (Art 15(a) DADP); a 12-year delay attributable to A would equally dispense with it (Art 15(b)).
• Rule: customary (Interhandel 1959; ELSI 1989; Art 14 DADP; admissibility condition, Art 44(b) ARSIWA) – all available remedies up to the highest instance must be used so that the state can redress the wrong within its own system.
• Exceptions (Art 15 DADP): (a) no reasonably available remedy providing effective redress (futility – not mere doubt about the chances; here a statutory bar plus settled case law); (b) undue delay attributable to the responsible state; (c) no relevant connection with that state at the date of injury; (d) the person is manifestly precluded from pursuing remedies; (e) waiver by the responsible state.
• No exhaustion is needed where the state itself is directly injured (its embassy, warship); ICJ jurisdiction still requires a basis.
Memorise: exhaust all (Interhandel/ELSI, Art 14) · exceptions Art 15: futile · delay · no connection · precluded · waived · direct injury to the state → no exhaustion.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Variant of a diplomatic-protection case: the destroyed equipment belonged not to Joelle but to NewsCo, a TV company incorporated and registered in State D. 90% of NewsCo's shares are held by nationals of State B (including Joelle), and its management sits in State B. State A destroyed the equipment and bans NewsCo from reporting. Who may exercise diplomatic protection for NewsCo? Can B protect the shareholders? Would it differ if NewsCo had been dissolved under D's law, or if A had required incorporation in A as a condition for working there? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: In principle only D, the state of incorporation (Barcelona Traction 1970; Art 9 DADP); B may protect the company only if NewsCo has no substantial business in D and both its seat of management and financial control are in B; B may protect the shareholders only under the exceptions of Art 11 or for their own direct rights (Diallo).
• Barcelona Traction (Belgium v Spain, ICJ 1970): Belgium, the state of about 88% of the shareholders of a Canadian company injured by Spain, lacked standing – only the company's rights were affected; protection belongs to the state of incorporation and registered office (avoids multiple claims).
• Art 9 DADP: state of incorporation; but if the company is controlled by nationals of another state, has no substantial business in the state of incorporation, and its seat of management and financial control are both in another state, that state counts.
• Art 11 DADP – shareholders' state only if (a) the company has ceased to exist under the law of incorporation for a reason unrelated to the injury, or (b) it had the nationality of the responsible state and incorporation there was a precondition for doing business there – both variants of the question fall under these exceptions.
• Direct rights of shareholders (dividends, voting, management) may be protected by their own state (Art 12; Diallo, Guinea v DRC 2007/2010 – 'protection by substitution' is not custom). Joelle's own detention can in any case be protected by B; investment treaties may give shareholders their own claims (Art 17 DADP).
Memorise: company = state of incorporation (Barcelona Traction, Art 9) · exception: no business + seat + control elsewhere · shareholders only Art 11 (company extinct / forced local incorporation) · own rights Art 12 (Diallo) · BITs.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Variant of a diplomatic-protection case: Joelle, a national of State A by birth living in State B, is detained and mistreated in State A in 2025. Six months after her release she is naturalised in State B, keeping A's nationality, and asks B to present a claim against A. Can B exercise diplomatic protection? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – the claim requires B's nationality continuously from the date of injury to the official presentation of the claim (Art 5(1) DADP); Joelle acquired it only after the injury, and none of the exceptions applies.
• Purpose: preventing 'nationality shopping' for a powerful protector.
• Art 5(2) exception only if the person had a predecessor state's nationality, or lost the previous nationality and acquired the new one for a reason unrelated to the claim (e.g., marriage) – Joelle kept A's nationality.
• Art 5(3): never against a former state of nationality for an injury suffered while its national; against a current state of nationality Art 7 predominance would also be required.
Memorise: continuous nationality injury → presentation (Art 5(1)) · exception only for loss + unrelated acquisition/succession (Art 5(2)) · never against the former national state (Art 5(3)).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Tomas, a national of State T, is arrested in State U and sentenced to death without being informed of his right to have T's consulate notified; T's consul learns of the case only after the trial. Distinguish consular assistance from diplomatic protection and assess T's options. Would it differ if Tomas were also a national of State U? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Consular assistance is preventive help for nationals abroad under the 1963 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations (Art 36) and presupposes neither a completed wrongful act nor exhaustion of local remedies; diplomatic protection is the invocation of responsibility for a completed wrong. U has breached Art 36 VCCR, and T may invoke U's responsibility, including before the ICJ.
• Art 36(1) VCCR: free communication and access; the authorities must inform the detainee without delay of his right to have the consulate notified and notify it at his request; consuls may visit him and arrange legal representation.
• LaGrand (Germany v USA, ICJ 2001): Art 36 creates individual rights which the national state may invoke; ICJ provisional measures are binding. Avena (Mexico v USA 2004): effective review and reconsideration of conviction and sentence; similarly Jadhav (India v Pakistan 2019).
• Differences: consular assistance – consular function (Art 5 VCCR), preventive, no injury required; diplomatic protection – claim for a completed wrongful act, subject to nationality of claims and local remedies (Arts 1, 14 DADP); the two are independent (Art 16 DADP).
• T's options: invoke U's breach (police and courts, Art 4 ARSIWA) – cessation, review and reconsideration, assurances of non-repetition; ICJ if jurisdiction exists (Optional Protocol to the VCCR).
• Dual national of U: U may treat him as its own national (Art 3 Hague Convention 1930), so consular access is generally not owed; protection against U would require predominance of T's nationality (Art 7 DADP).
Memorise: consular (VCCR Art 36: inform, notify, visit – preventive) vs DP (after the wrong, nationality + local remedies) · LaGrand 2001 individual rights · Avena 2004 review and reconsideration · dual national: receiving state may treat as own.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: What is the legal basis of state immunity? Explain the difference between absolute and restrictive immunity and how acta iure imperii are distinguished from acta iure gestionis. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: State immunity (par in parem non habet imperium) shields a foreign state from the jurisdiction of domestic courts; under the absolute theory every act was covered, under the now prevailing restrictive theory only sovereign acts (acta iure imperii) are, while private or commercial acts (acta iure gestionis) are not; the distinction turns primarily on the nature of the act.
• Basis: sovereign equality (Art 2(1) UN Charter); customary law (Jurisdictional Immunities of the State, ICJ 2012); European Convention on State Immunity 1972 (few parties, including Austria); UN Convention on Jurisdictional Immunities of States and Their Property 2004 (UNCSI – not yet in force, 30 ratifications needed, but largely reflecting custom); national statutes (US FSIA 1976, UK SIA 1978).
• Absolute theory: no foreign state may be sued at all. With state trading, courts moved to the restrictive theory – in Austria the OGH in the Dralle case (1950): acta gestionis are no longer excluded from domestic jurisdiction.
• Nature test: could a private person do it? Sale, lease, loan, construction contracts = gestionis; legislation, police, military action, expropriation, diplomacy = imperii. Purpose test: what the act serves (army boots would be sovereign). Art 2(2) UNCSI: primarily nature, purpose only if agreed or relevant in the forum's practice; Empire of Iran (BVerfG 1963): repair of the embassy heating = commercial.
• Codified exceptions (UNCSI): commercial transactions (Art 10), employment contracts (Art 11), personal injury and property damage in the forum (Art 12), immovable property, commercial ships, arbitration; consent or waiver (Arts 7–8).
Memorise: par in parem · absolute → restrictive (Dralle 1950) · imperii immune vs gestionis not · nature > purpose (Art 2(2) UNCSI; Empire of Iran 1963) · UNCSI 2004 not in force = custom.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: The embassy of State F in Vienna orders a new heating system from the Austrian company Wärme GmbH and does not pay. Wärme sues State F before the Austrian courts, wins, and then seeks to enforce the judgment against (1) the embassy's bank account used for salaries and rent, (2) a building owned by F in Vienna rented out as offices to private companies, and (3) reserves of F's central bank deposited in Austria. Assess immunity from jurisdiction and from enforcement. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: F enjoys no immunity from jurisdiction – ordering a heating system is by its nature a commercial act; immunity from enforcement is a separate question: the embassy account and the central bank reserves are immune, the commercially rented building may be seized.
• Jurisdiction: restrictive immunity; the nature of the act decides – a contract for work that any private person could conclude; its embassy purpose does not make it sovereign (Empire of Iran, BVerfG 1963 – repair of the embassy heating; Art 10 UNCSI).
• Enforcement turns on the purpose of the assets at the time execution begins: property serving sovereign (governmental, non-commercial) purposes is immune without the state's consent, even if the judgment concerns an actum iure gestionis (BVerfG, Philippine Embassy 1977; Art 19 UNCSI: constraint only with consent, on allocated property, or on property in use or intended for use for other than governmental non-commercial purposes, located in the forum and connected with the entity sued).
• (1) Embassy account: serves the functioning of the mission → immune; mixed accounts are protected as a whole and F cannot be required to disclose the uses (Philippine Embassy 1977; Art 21(1)(a) UNCSI; mission property also protected by Art 22(3) VCDR).
• (2) Building rented out commercially → commercial purpose → execution possible.
• (3) Central bank property: special category presumed non-commercial (Art 21(1)(c) UNCSI) → immune.
• A waiver of jurisdiction is not a waiver of enforcement (Art 20 UNCSI).
Memorise: jurisdiction = nature of the act (Empire of Iran) · enforcement = purpose of the asset at execution (Philippine Embassy) · protected: mission accounts, central bank, military, cultural property (Art 21 UNCSI).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Relatives of civilians massacred in 1944 by the armed forces of State G during its occupation of State I sue G before the courts of State I. The Supreme Court of I denies G immunity because (1) the acts took place on I's territory, (2) they violated ius cogens, and (3) the victims have no other remedy. I's courts then register a judicial mortgage on a villa owned by G in I that serves as a cultural exchange centre. Assess under international law. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: I violates G's immunity: acts of armed forces in an armed conflict are acta iure imperii covered by customary immunity regardless of their unlawfulness; neither the territorial tort exception nor ius cogens nor the 'last resort' argument removes immunity, and the mortgage on property used for governmental non-commercial purposes breaches immunity from enforcement (Jurisdictional Immunities of the State, Germany v Italy, ICJ 2012).
• Immunity is customary and procedural; a massacre by armed forces is a sovereign act by its nature – its illegality does not change its sovereign character (German Federal Constitutional Court in the Distomo litigation, 2006).
• (1) Tort exception (Art 12 UNCSI; Art 11 European Convention): under customary law it does not extend to acts of armed forces during an armed conflict (ICJ 2012). The Greek Areios Pagos held otherwise in Distomo (2000), but its judgment was never enforced and the Greek Special Supreme Court later affirmed immunity (Margellos 2002).
• (2) Ius cogens: no conflict – ius cogens concerns the substantive prohibition (killing civilians), immunity concerns whether a forum may hear the case; hence no hierarchy-based exception (ICJ 2012; Al-Adsani v UK, ECtHR 2001).
• (3) Last resort: no recognised exception; the question of reparation must be settled between the states.
• Enforcement: the villa (Villa Vigoni) served governmental non-commercial purposes → measures of constraint violate immunity; granting exequatur to foreign judgments (the Greek Distomo judgment) was also a violation.
• Consequences: the court decisions are acts of I (Art 4 ARSIWA); I must ensure that they cease to have effect (by legislation or other means). Aftermath: the Italian Constitutional Court (judgment 238/2014) refused to follow; Germany instituted new ICJ proceedings in 2022.
Memorise: Germany v Italy 2012 · armed forces in armed conflict = imperii · no tort / ius cogens / last-resort exception (procedure ≠ substance) · enforcement: Villa Vigoni · Distomo: Greece 2000 vs Germany 2006.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: The large state of Willunia dissolves. The small successor state Selenur announces that its courts will no longer grant immunity to foreign states, even for acts performed in the exercise of sovereign authority. It argues (i) that as a new state it starts with a clean slate and (ii) that it has criticised immunity since its founding. A Selenurian court then admits a claim against neighbouring Cornistan concerning the conduct of Cornistan's border police. Assess. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Selenur is bound by the customary rule of state immunity: the clean slate principle concerns only treaties of newly independent states, and a persistent objector must object while a rule is emerging; admitting the claim about Cornistan's border police (actum iure imperii) is an internationally wrongful act of Selenur.
• Immunity: customary rule based on sovereign equality (par in parem non habet imperium; Germany v Italy 2012), in its restrictive form – police and border control are classic sovereign acts.
• New states and custom: a new state enters an existing legal order and is bound by general customary law from its birth. The clean slate (Art 16 VCST) concerns only treaties and only newly independent states from decolonisation; Selenur emerged from a dissolution (treaties would even continue under Art 34).
• Persistent objector: only a state that objects persistently, consistently and clearly while the rule is forming is exempt (Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries 1951; ILC Conclusions on Identification of Customary International Law 2018, conclusion 15); immunity was settled long before Selenur existed → impossible.
• What Selenur may do: deny immunity for acta iure gestionis (restrictive theory), negotiate treaties, promote a change of the rule – at the risk of breaching it.
• Consequences: the court's decision is attributable to Selenur (Art 4 ARSIWA – judiciary); Cornistan may demand cessation (non-enforcement, annulment), protest, seize a court if jurisdiction exists, or take proportionate non-forcible countermeasures (Arts 49–54 ARSIWA).
Memorise: new state = bound by existing custom · clean slate = treaties only (Art 16 VCST) · persistent objector only during formation · border police = imperii · court judgment = act of the state (Art 4).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: An investigating judge of State J issues and circulates via Interpol an international arrest warrant for crimes against humanity against the incumbent foreign minister of State K. Two years later, when he has left office, J wants to prosecute him for the same acts, committed in his official capacity, and for private tax fraud committed while he was in office. Assess. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: While in office the foreign minister enjoys full immunity ratione personae and inviolability from foreign criminal jurisdiction, even for international crimes – issuing and circulating the warrant violated K's rights (Arrest Warrant, ICJ 2002); after leaving office he keeps only immunity ratione materiae for official acts, which does not cover private acts and, on a growing view, not international crimes.
• Ratione personae: the 'troika' – head of state, head of government, foreign minister (and diplomats) – full immunity from criminal jurisdiction and inviolability abroad for all acts, official or private, to ensure the performance of their functions; no customary exception for international crimes (Arrest Warrant, DRC v Belgium 2002 – Yerodia; issuing and circulating the warrant was itself a violation, Belgium had to cancel it). Ends with the office.
• Ratione materiae: all state officials for official acts, continuing after office – in substance the state's own immunity.
• Immunity ≠ impunity (Arrest Warrant, para 61): prosecution (1) in his own state, (2) after waiver by K, (3) after office for acts before or after office and private acts during office, (4) before an international criminal court with jurisdiction (Art 27 Rome Statute).
• After office: tax fraud = private act → no immunity. Crimes against humanity in an official capacity → contested: Pinochet (House of Lords 1999) denied functional immunity for torture; ILC Draft Article 7 on Immunity of State Officials (first reading 2022) excludes it for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture etc. – not settled custom.
Memorise: ratione personae = troika + diplomats, all acts, only during office (Arrest Warrant 2002) · ratione materiae = official acts of all officials, lasting · four ways around impunity · international-crimes exception contested (Pinochet, ILC Draft Art 7).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: After a private party, diplomat D of State S's embassy in Vienna drives while drunk and seriously injures a cyclist. The Austrian police want to arrest D and search his private residence for evidence; the cyclist sues D for damages before an Austrian civil court. What protection does D enjoy under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, and what can Austria do? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: D enjoys personal inviolability and complete immunity from criminal jurisdiction, and also immunity from civil jurisdiction because a private traffic accident falls under none of the exceptions; his residence is inviolable; Austria can request an express waiver from S, declare D persona non grata, or rely on S's own jurisdiction.
• Personal inviolability (Art 29 VCDR): no arrest or detention in any form; the police may only avert immediate danger (e.g., stop him from driving on).
• Private residence inviolable (Art 30), like the mission premises (Art 22): no entry or search without consent.
• Jurisdiction (Art 31): criminal immunity absolute; civil immunity except (a) real actions on private immovable property in the receiving state, (b) succession matters as a private person, (c) professional or commercial activity outside his functions → the damages claim is inadmissible (contrast consular officers: no immunity for vehicle accident claims, Art 43(2)(b) VCCR). He remains subject to S's jurisdiction (Art 31(4)) and must respect local law (Art 41).
• Waiver (Art 32): only by S, always express; a separate waiver is needed for execution of a civil judgment.
• Persona non grata (Art 9): at any time, without reasons; S must recall him; after a reasonable period his immunity ends except for official acts (Art 39(2)). Diplomatic law is a self-contained regime (Tehran Hostages 1980). Practically, the victim claims against the motor insurer.
Memorise: Art 29 person · Art 30 residence · Art 31 criminal absolute, civil except property/succession/commerce · Art 32 waiver express, execution separate · Art 9 persona non grata · Art 39(2) residual immunity for official acts.

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: At State R's embassy in Vienna: (1) the 17-year-old son of the counsellor (not an Austrian national) is caught shoplifting; (2) the embassy's IT technician, a member of the administrative and technical staff and a national of R, causes an accident while driving to a private dinner; (3) a second secretary who is an Austrian national is sued for unpaid rent for his private flat; (4) the ambassador's private cook is charged with assault. Who enjoys immunity under the VCDR? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) the son – full diplomatic immunity as a family member; (2) the technician – criminal immunity, but no civil immunity for acts outside his duties; (3) the Austrian second secretary – immunity only for official acts, so the rent claim may proceed; (4) the cook – no immunity except as Austria may grant.
• Art 37(1): members of the family forming part of the diplomat's household, if not nationals of the receiving state, enjoy the privileges and immunities of Arts 29–36 → the son is inviolable and immune; Austria may request a waiver or declare him persona non grata.
• Art 37(2): administrative and technical staff (not nationals or permanent residents) enjoy Arts 29–35, i.e., full criminal immunity, but civil and administrative immunity does not extend to acts performed outside the course of their duties → civil claim for the private accident admissible, no prosecution.
• Art 38(1): a diplomatic agent who is a national of or permanently resident in the receiving state enjoys only immunity from jurisdiction and inviolability in respect of official acts performed in the exercise of his functions (unless more is granted) → the private rent claim may proceed.
• Art 37(3): service staff – immunity only for acts performed in the course of their duties; Art 37(4): private servants – privileges only to the extent admitted by the receiving state, which must exercise jurisdiction without unduly interfering with the mission → the cook can be prosecuted.
Memorise: diplomat & family = full (Art 37(1)) · admin-tech = criminal full, civil only official acts (37(2)) · service staff = official acts (37(3)) · private servants = nothing by right (37(4)) · own nationals = official acts only (Art 38).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: An opposition journalist wanted by the police of State Dorvia flees into the embassy of State E in Dorvia's capital. Dorvian police want to enter the embassy to arrest him; after E refuses, Dorvia cuts off the embassy's electricity and threatens to storm it. E claims a right to grant diplomatic asylum. Assess. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Dorvian agents may not enter without the consent of the head of mission (Art 22 VCDR), not even to arrest a fugitive, and Dorvia must protect the premises; but E has no general right under universal international law to grant diplomatic asylum; Dorvia's lawful reactions are negotiation, persona non grata or breaking off relations.
• Art 22 VCDR: premises inviolable – no entry without the head of mission's consent, no exception for emergencies or suspects (contrast consular premises, Art 31(2) VCCR: consent assumed for fire or disaster); special duty to protect them; no search, requisition, attachment or execution.
