• Cutting utilities and threatening a raid breach Arts 22 and 25 VCDR (cf. Ecuador's raid on Mexico's embassy in Quito, April 2024, widely condemned and brought before the ICJ).
• Diplomatic asylum: no general customary right (Asylum case, Colombia v Peru, ICJ 1950), only regional Latin American conventions; sheltering a fugitive may breach Art 41, but even misuse does not allow entry (Assange in Ecuador's London embassy 2012–2019, arrested only after Ecuador's consent).
• Inviolability is not extraterritoriality: the premises remain Dorvian territory, but Dorvian law cannot be enforced there.
Memorise: Art 22 inviolable premises – no entry without consent, even for fugitives · no general diplomatic asylum (Asylum case 1950) · inviolability ≠ extraterritoriality · remedies: persona non grata, breaking relations (self-contained regime).

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Anna, an Austrian national, works as a receptionist and translator at State M's embassy in Vienna. After her dismissal she sues State M before the Austrian labour court for unpaid wages and for reinstatement. Her colleague Boris, a national of M serving as political counsellor (diplomatic agent), also sues M over his dismissal. May M invoke state immunity? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Anna's wage claim may proceed – employing local auxiliary staff is not a sovereign act (Art 11 UNCSI) – but her claim for reinstatement is barred; Boris's claim is barred because he is a diplomatic agent exercising governmental functions and a national of M.
• Art 11(1) UNCSI (reflecting custom in this respect): no immunity in proceedings relating to an employment contract for work performed in the forum state.
• Exceptions (Art 11(2)): functions in the exercise of governmental authority; diplomatic agents and consular officers; proceedings on recruitment, renewal or reinstatement; dismissal where the head of state, government or foreign minister certifies security interests; employee a national of the employer state (unless permanently resident in the forum).
• ECtHR: immunity beyond customary law violates access to court (Art 6 ECHR) – Cudak v Lithuania 2010 (switchboard operator), Sabeh El Leil v France 2011 (accountant).
• Application: Anna's auxiliary tasks are not sovereign → wage claim admissible, reinstatement immune. Boris → immune (diplomatic agent and national of M). Enforcement of any judgment is a separate question (embassy accounts).
Memorise: employment (Art 11 UNCSI) = no immunity except governmental functions, diplomats, reinstatement, security, employer-state nationals · Cudak 2010, Sabeh El Leil 2011 · enforcement separate.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: What is the difference between state responsibility and liability under international law? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: State responsibility is the legal consequence of an internationally wrongful act (conduct attributable to a state that breaches an international obligation); liability is the duty to compensate damage caused by lawful but hazardous activities, without any breach, and exists only where a treaty provides for it.
• Responsibility: ARSIWA 2001 – attribution + breach, no general fault or damage requirement; consequences cessation and full reparation (Chorzów). Example: unlawful detention of a foreign diplomat.
• Liability (sine delicto): space objects (Liability Convention 1972, Art II: absolute liability of the launching state for damage on the earth's surface or to aircraft in flight – Cosmos 954, Canada 1978), nuclear installations (Paris 1960, Vienna 1963 – operator liability, state as guarantor), oil pollution; the ILC Principles on the Allocation of Loss (2006) are soft law. Consequence: compensation only, often capped.
• A breach of the due-diligence duty to prevent harm (Trail Smelter 1941; Pulp Mills 2010) is responsibility, not liability.
Memorise: responsibility = unlawful act (ARSIWA) · liability = lawful but dangerous activity, treaty-based (Liability Convention 1972 Art II) · due-diligence breach = responsibility.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: What conduct is attributed to a state in the context of state responsibility? (6 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Attributed are the conduct of the state's organs (Art 4 ARSIWA), of persons or entities empowered to exercise governmental authority (Art 5), of organs placed at its disposal by another state (Art 6) – even when acting ultra vires (Art 7) –, of private persons acting on its instructions or under its direction or effective control (Art 8), of persons exercising governmental authority in the absence of the authorities (Art 9), of successful insurrectional movements (Art 10), and conduct the state acknowledges and adopts as its own (Art 11).
• Principle: a state acts only through human beings; private conduct as such is not attributable (the state may still answer for its own omission – lack of due diligence).
• Art 4 – organs: legislative, executive, judicial or other, whatever their position (central or territorial unit, e.g., the governor of Arizona in LaGrand) and rank; de iure organs and de facto organs acting in complete dependence (Nicaragua 1986; Bosnian Genocide 2007).
• Art 5 – entities empowered by law to exercise elements of governmental authority, acting in that capacity (private prisons, airlines doing immigration control) – outsourcing does not shed responsibility.
• Art 6 – organ of another state placed at its disposal and acting under its authority.
• Art 7 – ultra vires: attributable even if the organ exceeds its authority or disobeys instructions, as long as it acts in official capacity (Caire 1929); purely private off-duty conduct is not.
• Art 8 – private persons acting on the state's instructions or under its effective control of the specific operation (Nicaragua 1986; Bosnian Genocide 2007 rejected Tadić's overall control, 1999).
• Art 9 – governmental authority exercised in the absence or default of the official authorities (Yeager v Iran 1987).
• Art 10 – insurrectional movement becoming the new government (→ the state) or founding a new state (→ that state); failed rebels are not attributable.
• Art 11 – conduct clearly acknowledged and adopted by the state as its own (Tehran Hostages 1980).
• Beyond attribution: aid or assistance, direction and control, coercion of another state's wrongful act (Arts 16–18).
Memorise: 4 organs · 5 governmental authority · 6 lent organs · 7 ultra vires · 8 instructions/effective control · 9 absence of authorities · 10 insurgents · 11 adoption · (16–18 complicity).

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: Where is the regime of state responsibility under international law regulated? Which body adopted the text? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: In customary international law, codified in the Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (ARSIWA), adopted by the International Law Commission (ILC) in 2001; the UN General Assembly took note of them (Res 56/83 of 12 Dec 2001) – they are not a treaty.
• ILC: expert body of the General Assembly for codification and progressive development (Art 13(1)(a) UN Charter); last Special Rapporteur James Crawford.
• Status: annexed to a GA resolution and commended to governments, no convention concluded – not binding as such, but largely reflecting custom and applied as authoritative by the ICJ (e.g., Arts 4 and 8 in Bosnian Genocide 2007).
• Structure: Part One wrongful act, Part Two content (cessation, reparation), Part Three implementation (invocation, countermeasures); lex specialis prevails (Art 55). Companion text for IOs: ARIO 2011.
Memorise: ARSIWA 2001 · ILC · GA took note (Res 56/83) · not a treaty, customary law · lex specialis Art 55.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'A state is responsible under international law only if it acted with fault and caused material damage.' Give reasons. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No – responsibility arises from every internationally wrongful act, i.e., conduct attributable to a state that breaches an international obligation (Arts 1–2 ARSIWA), without a general requirement of fault or damage, provided no circumstance precludes wrongfulness.
• Art 1: every internationally wrongful act entails responsibility. Art 2: conduct (act or omission) that (a) is attributable to the state and (b) breaches an international obligation – of whatever origin, treaty or custom (Art 12). Art 3: the characterisation is governed by international law, not internal law.
• Fault: no general element (objective responsibility); it depends on the primary rule – some require knowledge or due diligence (Corfu Channel 1949: Albania knew of the mines; duty to prevent genocide) or intent (genocide's special intent).
• Damage: not an element – the breach of an obligation owed to a state is itself a legal injury (Rainbow Warrior 1990). Damage matters for reparation (injury includes material and moral damage, Art 31) and for identifying the injured state (Art 42).
• Negative element: no circumstance precluding wrongfulness (Arts 20–25).
• Nature: civil and compensatory, not criminal – the 'international crimes of states' of the 1976 draft were dropped; instead special consequences for serious breaches of peremptory norms (Arts 40–41).
Memorise: wrongful act = attribution + breach (Art 2) − justification · no fault, no damage as general elements · damage → reparation.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: (1) A customs officer of State P, in uniform at his border post, beats up a foreign truck driver, in breach of explicit service instructions. (2) The same evening, off duty and in civilian clothes, he assaults a foreign tourist in a bar. (3) A private security company, entrusted by P's law with passport control at the airport, unlawfully detains a foreign journalist for two days. Which conduct is attributable to State P? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (1) and (3) are attributable – an ultra vires act of an organ acting in its official capacity (Arts 4, 7 ARSIWA) and conduct of an entity exercising governmental authority (Arts 5, 7); (2) is a private act and not attributable – P is responsible only if it fails to investigate and punish.
• Art 4: the officer is a state organ. Art 7: conduct of an organ or of an Art 5 entity acting in that capacity is attributable even if it exceeds authority or contravenes instructions – otherwise states could escape responsibility through internal instructions (Caire 1929; Youmans 1926). Test: acting with apparent authority / under colour of office (uniform, at his post, using his powers).
• (2) Off-duty conduct as a private individual is not conduct 'in that capacity' → not attributable; P's own duty of due diligence: investigate, prosecute, provide remedies (otherwise denial of justice).
• (3) Art 5: an entity that is not an organ but empowered by law to exercise elements of governmental authority (passport control is sovereign) → attributable when acting in that capacity, ultra vires included (Art 7).
• Consequence: P owes reparation; the victims' states may exercise diplomatic protection after exhaustion of local remedies.
Memorise: organ + official capacity → attributable even ultra vires (Art 7, Caire) · off-duty private act → not attributable (only due diligence) · Art 5 outsourced governmental authority.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: State Z finances, arms and trains the rebel 'Liberation Front' in neighbouring State W and helps coordinate its general military planning; Z's advisers do not direct specific operations. The Front massacres the civilians of a village in W. W claims that Z is responsible for the massacre. Assess. Would it differ if a general of Z had ordered the attack on that village? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Under Art 8 ARSIWA as interpreted by the ICJ, the massacre is attributable to Z only if Z exercised effective control over the specific operation (Nicaragua 1986; Bosnian Genocide 2007) – general support and coordination ('overall control') is not enough; if Z's general ordered the attack, it is attributable (instructions).
• Art 8: conduct of persons or groups acting on the instructions of, or under the direction or control of, the state in carrying out the conduct.
• Nicaragua v USA (1986): US financing, organising, training, supplying and equipping of the contras, the selection of targets and planning of operations were insufficient; the US would have to have had effective control of the operations in the course of which the violations were committed.
• Tadić (ICTY Appeals Chamber 1999): 'overall control' (financing, equipping, coordinating or helping in general planning) suffices for organised armed groups – but that test served to classify the conflict as international under humanitarian law.
• Bosnian Genocide (2007): the ICJ rejected overall control for state responsibility; Srebrenica was not attributable to the FRY (no complete dependence of the perpetrators, no effective control), but the FRY was responsible for failing to prevent genocide and to cooperate with the ICTY.
• De facto organ route (Art 4): only if the group acts in complete dependence, as a mere instrument – not the case here.
• Z is responsible anyway for its own acts: support of rebels violates non-intervention and, through arming and training, the prohibition of force (Nicaragua).
• Variant: an order by Z's general = instructions → attributable to Z.
Memorise: effective control (Nicaragua 1986, Bosnian Genocide 2007) vs overall control (Tadić 1999, IHL classification) · complete dependence = de facto organ · support alone = intervention, not attribution.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: Students storm the embassy of State U in State Iria and take the diplomats hostage; Iria's police, present nearby, do nothing. Two weeks later Iria's head of state issues a decree approving the occupation and ordering that the hostages be held until U extradites Iria's former ruler. Is Iria responsible – from when and why? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes – at first not for the students' acts (not attributable) but for its own failure to protect the embassy and the diplomats (Arts 22, 29 VCDR); from the decree onwards the continued occupation is Iria's own act by acknowledgment and adoption (Art 11 ARSIWA; Tehran Hostages, ICJ 1980).
• Phase 1: the militants were neither organs nor acting on instructions or under effective control (Art 8); general statements of sympathy do not suffice. But Iria was under a special duty to take all appropriate steps to protect the premises and the diplomats (Arts 22(2), 29 VCDR); its police's inaction is a wrongful omission attributable under Art 4.
• Phase 2: the decree (in the real case: Ayatollah Khomeini's decree of 17 Nov 1979) translated approval into state policy – the continuing occupation and detention became acts of the state (Art 11: to the extent the state acknowledges and adopts the conduct as its own; this must be clear and unequivocal – mere approval or endorsement is not enough).
• No justification as a countermeasure against alleged wrongs of U: diplomatic law is a self-contained regime with its own remedies (persona non grata, breaking off relations), and countermeasures may not affect diplomatic inviolability (Art 50(2)(b) ARSIWA).
• Consequences: cessation (release of the hostages), restoration of the premises, reparation.
Memorise: Tehran 1980: phase 1 = own omission (due diligence, Arts 22/29 VCDR) · phase 2 = adoption (Art 11) · diplomatic law = self-contained regime · Art 50(2)(b).

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: During a civil war in State Kasar, rebels of the 'People's Army' destroy a foreign-owned factory in 2023. Who is responsible if (a) in 2025 the rebels win and form the new government of Kasar, (b) they instead establish a new state, 'Eastern Kasar', in the region where the factory stood, or (c) they are defeated? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Kasar – the conduct of an insurrectional movement that becomes the new government is attributed to the state (Art 10(1) ARSIWA); (b) the new state Eastern Kasar (Art 10(2)); (c) the rebels' acts are not attributable to Kasar – it is responsible only for its own failure of due diligence.
• Rationale: continuity between the movement and the later government or new state; conversely a state cannot answer for those fighting to overthrow it.
• (c) Failed rebels: Kasar answers only for its own conduct (Art 10(3)) – e.g., if its forces could have protected the factory and did not, or it failed to investigate and prosecute; the rebels themselves may bear individual criminal responsibility (war crimes).
• Related: Art 9 – persons exercising governmental authority in the absence or default of the official authorities.
• Enforcement: the owner's state may exercise diplomatic protection.
Memorise: Art 10: rebels → new government: state responsible · → new state: new state responsible · defeated: not attributable (only own due diligence).

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: Name and explain the circumstances precluding wrongfulness under the ILC Articles on State Responsibility. Which limits apply to all of them? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Consent (Art 20), self-defence (Art 21), countermeasures (Art 22), force majeure (Art 23), distress (Art 24) and necessity (Art 25); none can justify a breach of a peremptory norm (Art 26), and they are without prejudice to compliance once the circumstance ceases and to compensation for material loss (Art 27).
• Consent (Art 20): valid consent of the competent authority, freely given before or during the act, and only within its limits (e.g., allowing foreign officials to make an arrest on its territory); only where the rule permits it – consent cannot legalise a breach of a peremptory norm such as aggression (Art 26); an invitation by the government means there is no use of force against the state at all, rebels cannot validly consent (Nicaragua).
• Self-defence (Art 21): a lawful measure in conformity with the Charter (Art 51) precludes the wrongfulness of non-performance of other obligations towards the aggressor – not of humanitarian law or non-derogable human rights.
• Countermeasures (Art 22; Arts 49–54): non-forcible response to a prior wrongful act to induce compliance.
• Force majeure (Art 23): irresistible force or unforeseen event beyond control making performance materially impossible (aircraft forced into foreign airspace by a storm); not if the state contributed or assumed the risk; mere difficulty is not enough (Rainbow Warrior 1990).
• Distress (Art 24): the author has no other reasonable way to save his own life or the lives of persons in his care (ship entering a foreign port in a storm); not if caused by the state or creating a comparable or greater peril.
• Necessity (Art 25): the only way to safeguard an essential interest against a grave and imminent peril, without seriously impairing an essential interest of the other state(s) or the international community; excluded if the obligation rules it out or the state contributed (Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros 1997).
• Common limits: Art 26 (ius cogens); Art 27 (obligation revives, compensation for material loss).
Memorise: Consent · Self-defence · Countermeasures · Force majeure · Distress · Necessity (Arts 20–25) · Art 26 ius cogens · Art 27 revival + compensation.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: Under a 1977 treaty, States H and S agreed to build a joint barrage system on their border river. In 1989 H suspends and then abandons the works, citing possible long-term ecological risks for its drinking water; S reacts by unilaterally diverting about 80% of the river's flow into a canal on its own territory. Assess H's plea of necessity and the legality of S's reaction. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: H's plea of necessity fails – the ecological danger was not established as a grave and imminent peril and other means were available; S's diversion is no lawful countermeasure because it is disproportionate; both committed wrongful acts and the treaty remains in force (Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros, Hungary/Slovakia, ICJ 1997).
• Necessity (customary; now Art 25 ARSIWA): exceptional and strictly limited; cumulative conditions – an essential interest (the environment can be one); a grave and imminent peril (a merely possible, uncertain long-term risk is insufficient; a long-term peril can be imminent only if it is certain and inevitable); the act is the only means; no serious impairment of the other state's essential interest; no contribution by the invoking state. Hungary failed on imminence and on alternative means.
• Effect: necessity only precludes wrongfulness – it does not terminate the treaty; the obligations revive (Art 27) and compensation may be owed.
• S's diversion as a countermeasure: requires a prior wrongful act (yes), direction against the wrongdoer, a prior call to comply, and proportionality – depriving H of its right to an equitable and reasonable share of a shared river is not proportionate → unlawful.
• Succession: the 1977 treaty established a territorial regime (Art 12 VCST, customary) and survived the dissolution of Czechoslovakia, binding Slovakia.
• Outcome: the parties must negotiate in good faith; mutual compensation.
Memorise: Gabčíkovo 1997 · necessity = only way + grave & imminent peril + no serious impairment + no contribution · necessity ≠ termination · countermeasure must be proportionate (Variant C was not).

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: (a) A military transport plane of State A, hit by a storm and suffering engine failure, is driven into State B's airspace and crash-lands. (b) The pilot of a State A patrol aircraft, lost and almost out of fuel, decides to land without permission at B's military airport to save the crew. (c) State A refuses to pay an instalment on a loan owed to State B, citing a severe economic crisis. Are these acts wrongful? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) force majeure precludes wrongfulness (Art 23 ARSIWA); (b) distress (Art 24), if there was no other reasonable way to save the crew; (c) financial difficulty is neither force majeure nor, as a rule, necessity – A remains responsible.
• Force majeure: involuntary conduct – irresistible force or unforeseen event beyond control making performance materially impossible; excluded if A contributed to it or assumed the risk.
• Distress: voluntary conduct, but no other reasonable way to save the author's life or persons in his care; excluded if caused by the state itself or if the act is likely to create a comparable or greater peril (e.g., an aircraft carrying nuclear weapons landing in a city). Rainbow Warrior (1990): France's evacuation of an officer for medical reasons was accepted in principle, but France breached its obligations by not returning him.
• (c) Performance is not materially impossible, only more burdensome; necessity only if its strict conditions are met (arbitral practice on Argentina's crisis mostly rejected it, e.g., CMS v Argentina 2005, because Argentina had contributed).
• Art 27: once the circumstance ends the obligation revives; compensation for material loss (e.g., damage caused by the crash) may still be due.
Memorise: force majeure = involuntary, material impossibility (Art 23) · distress = saving lives, no other way (Art 24) · money problems ≠ force majeure · Art 27 compensation.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: State R unlawfully seizes a merchant ship flying the flag of State S and still holds it after three months; the cargo is damaged, the owner loses a lucrative follow-up contract, and R's minister publicly insults S. What can S claim from R? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Cessation (release of the ship), assurances and guarantees of non-repetition if warranted, and full reparation – restitution (return of ship and cargo), compensation for the damaged cargo and the lost profit plus interest, and satisfaction for the immaterial injury (acknowledgment, apology).
• Legal consequences (Part Two ARSIWA): continued duty of performance (Art 29); cessation of the continuing wrongful act and appropriate assurances and guarantees of non-repetition (Art 30; LaGrand 2001).
• Full reparation (Art 31) – Chorzów Factory (PCIJ 1928): reparation must, as far as possible, wipe out all the consequences of the illegal act and re-establish the situation which would, in all probability, have existed if that act had not been committed. Forms (Art 34), in this order:
• Restitution (Art 35): re-establishing the prior situation, unless materially impossible or out of all proportion to compensation → release and return of the ship.
• Compensation (Art 36): financially assessable damage – damnum emergens (damaged cargo, costs) and lucrum cessans (lost contract, if sufficiently certain) – plus interest (Art 38) from the date the sum should have been paid.
• Satisfaction (Art 37): for non-material injury to S (insult, violation of its rights) – acknowledgment of the breach, expression of regret, formal apology, or a declaratory judgment (Corfu Channel 1949); not disproportionate or humiliating.
• Reduction for contributory fault (Art 39); internal law is no excuse (Art 32). As flag state, S may claim for the ship and everyone on board as a unit (M/V Saiga (No. 2), ITLOS 1999).
Memorise: cessation + non-repetition (Art 30) · Chorzów: wipe out all consequences · restitution → compensation (+ lost profit, interest) → satisfaction (Arts 35–38).

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: The border between Monturia and Lirania in a sparsely populated area has been unclear for decades. In 2022 Lirania built a mining facility in a disputed valley and has exploited its minerals ever since; Monturia protested at once but took no further action until it sued Lirania before the ICJ in 2025. Assume the Court finds that the valley belongs to Monturia. Did Monturia lose its title through its silence? What can it claim for the minerals extracted since 2022, and are interest and a time-bar an issue although no treaty regulates them? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Monturia kept its title – it protested, and three years of foreign possession are far too short for acquiescence or prescription; Lirania's mining is an internationally wrongful act, so Monturia can claim cessation and full reparation, i.e., compensation for the value of the extracted minerals plus interest (Art 38 ARSIWA, a general principle – no treaty needed); there is no fixed limitation period, and a three-year delay after a protest bars nothing.
• Title: acquiescence requires long silence where a reaction would have been called for (Temple of Preah Vihear 1962; Pedra Branca 2008); prescription requires long, peaceful, uncontested possession – Monturia's protest interrupts both.
• Wrongful act: a state mining facility exploiting resources on another state's territory violates its territorial sovereignty (attribution: Art 4 or 5 ARSIWA).
• Consequences: cessation – closing the facility (Art 30); restitution of the valley (Art 35); the minerals cannot be restored → compensation of their market value incl. lost profits (Art 36; Chorzów 1928); satisfaction for the violation of sovereignty (Art 37).
• Interest (Art 38): due where necessary for full reparation, from the date the sum should have been paid – a general principle of law, no treaty needed.
• Time-bar: no fixed limitation period in general international law; only unreasonable delay may lead to loss of the right by waiver or acquiescence (Art 45 ARSIWA; Certain Phosphate Lands in Nauru 1992). Protest in 2022, suit in 2025 → no loss.
Memorise: protest interrupts acquiescence/prescription · resource extraction on foreign territory = wrongful act · cessation + restitution + compensation (market value, lost profits) + satisfaction · interest Art 38 (general principle) · no fixed limitation, only Art 45 waiver/acquiescence.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: State M systematically tortures members of an ethnic minority and commits acts intended to destroy the group. State N, on another continent, has no affected nationals but wants to bring M before the ICJ, demanding cessation and reparation for the victims. Both are parties to the Genocide Convention and the Convention against Torture. M objects that N is not injured. Assess N's standing. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: N has standing as a non-injured state under Art 48 ARSIWA, because the obligations are owed erga omnes partes (to all parties to the conventions) and erga omnes (to the international community as a whole); it may claim cessation, assurances and reparation in the interest of the victims (Belgium v Senegal 2012; The Gambia v Myanmar 2022).
• Art 42 – injured state: obligation owed to it individually, or to a group/the community and the breach specially affects it or radically changes the position of all (integral obligations, e.g., disarmament) → N is not injured.
• Art 48(1) – any other state may invoke if the obligation (a) is owed to a group including it and protects a collective interest (erga omnes partes, e.g., human rights treaties) or (b) is owed to the international community as a whole (erga omnes – Barcelona Traction 1970, paras 33–34: aggression, genocide, slavery, racial discrimination; self-determination – East Timor 1995).
• Art 48(2): it may claim cessation, assurances of non-repetition and reparation in the interest of the injured state or the beneficiaries – not compensation for itself.
• ICJ: Belgium v Senegal (Habré, 2012) – every party to the Torture Convention may invoke; The Gambia v Myanmar (2022) – every party to the Genocide Convention; jurisdiction via Art IX Genocide Convention and Art 30 CAT. Collective countermeasures by non-injured states remain contested (Art 54: 'lawful measures').
Memorise: Art 42 injured (individually / specially affected / integral) vs Art 48 non-injured (erga omnes partes, erga omnes) → cessation + reparation for the victims · Barcelona Traction dictum · Belgium v Senegal 2012 · Gambia v Myanmar 2022.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: State X expropriates without compensation all assets of nationals of State Y. Y responds by (1) freezing the assets of X's state-owned trading company in Y, (2) suspending a bilateral trade treaty with X, (3) expelling X's ambassador, (4) searching X's embassy and seizing its archives, (5) threatening a naval blockade of X's ports, and (6) suspending fair-trial guarantees for X's nationals in Y. Which measures are lawful? (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Freezing the company's assets and suspending the trade treaty can be lawful countermeasures if the conditions are met; expelling the ambassador is lawful retorsion (persona non grata); searching the embassy and seizing its archives, threatening force and suspending human rights guarantees are prohibited.
• Countermeasures (Arts 22, 49–54 ARSIWA): conduct that would otherwise be unlawful, justified as a response to a prior wrongful act of the target state.
• Conditions: (a) a prior internationally wrongful act of X (uncompensated expropriation – yes); (b) directed only against X, to induce compliance, not to punish; temporary and as far as possible reversible (Art 49); (c) call on X to comply, notification of the decision and offer to negotiate (Art 52(1)) – urgent countermeasures allowed; (d) proportionality – commensurate with the injury, taking into account the gravity of the wrong and the rights in question (Art 51; Air Services 1978; Gabčíkovo 1997); (e) suspension while the dispute is pending before a court or tribunal with binding authority (Art 52(3)); (f) termination once X complies (Art 53).
• Prohibited (Art 50): threat or use of force; fundamental human rights; humanitarian prohibition of reprisals; other ius cogens; obligations under dispute settlement procedures; inviolability of diplomatic and consular agents, premises, archives and documents.
• (1) Freezing assets of a commercial state company – possible countermeasure if proportionate (assets of the state itself, e.g., central bank, raise immunity issues). (2) Suspension of the trade treaty – possible countermeasure (alternatively Art 60 VCLT if X materially breached that treaty). (3) Expulsion of the ambassador – retorsion: lawful though unfriendly (Art 9 VCDR), no justification needed. (4) Embassy search and archives – prohibited (Art 50(2)(b); Arts 22, 24 VCDR). (5) Blockade threat – prohibited (Art 50(1)(a); Art 2(4) UN Charter). (6) Fair-trial guarantees – prohibited (Art 50(1)(b)).
Memorise: countermeasure = prior wrong + against wrongdoer + to induce compliance + notice + proportionate + reversible · forbidden: force, human rights, humanitarian reprisals, ius cogens, diplomatic inviolability, dispute settlement · retorsion = lawful unfriendly act.

cards.topic: International Responsibility I — State Responsibility
cards.q: State D provides intelligence and air-to-air refuelling to State E's air force, knowing that E uses them to bomb hospitals in State F in violation of international humanitarian law. D's own planes never fire a shot. Is D responsible under international law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes – under Art 16 ARSIWA a state that aids or assists another state in committing a wrongful act is responsible if it does so with knowledge of the circumstances and the act would be wrongful if committed by itself; D answers for its own assistance, E for the bombing.
• Art 16 conditions: (a) knowledge of the circumstances of the wrongful act (the commentary also requires that the aid is given with a view to facilitating it); (b) the act would be wrongful if committed by the assisting state – the IHL rules protecting hospitals bind D as customary law.
• Related: Art 17 (direction and control over another state's wrongful act), Art 18 (coercion); for serious breaches of peremptory norms no state may render aid or assistance in maintaining the situation (Art 41(2)); common Art 1 Geneva Conventions: duty to ensure respect.
• Bosnian Genocide (2007): complicity in genocide requires at least knowledge of the specific genocidal intent; the FRY was not complicit but had failed to prevent.
• Consequences: D must cease the assistance and make reparation for its contribution; E remains fully responsible for its own act (plurality of responsible states, Art 47).
Memorise: Art 16 aid/assistance (knowledge + obligation binding the helper) · Art 17 direction and control · Art 18 coercion · Art 41(2) no aid for ius cogens breaches.

cards.topic: International Responsibility II — Organizations, Individuals, Liability
cards.q: Soldiers of State T serving in a UN peacekeeping mission established by the Security Council (operational command with the UN; T keeps disciplinary and criminal jurisdiction over its troops) detain civilians unlawfully and fail to protect them from a massacre. Victims want to hold someone responsible. Is the UN or State T responsible, and can they sue the UN in national courts? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The conduct is attributed to the entity with effective control over the specific conduct (Art 7 ARIO 2011): as a rule the UN, since peacekeepers under UN command act as UN subsidiary organs, but State T where it retained or exercised factual control (e.g., national orders) – dual attribution is possible; the UN itself enjoys immunity before national courts.
• ARIO 2011 (ILC; the GA took note): every wrongful act of an IO entails its responsibility (Art 3); conduct of its organs and agents is attributable (Art 6); a state organ placed at the IO's disposal is attributed to the IO if the IO exercises effective control over that conduct (Art 7); ultra vires acts included (Art 8).
• UN practice: peacekeepers are subsidiary organs; the UN pays compensation to third parties for their conduct, while contributing states keep disciplinary and criminal jurisdiction.
• Case law: ECtHR Behrami and Saramati (2007) attributed KFOR/UNMIK conduct in Kosovo to the UN because the Security Council retained 'ultimate authority and control' → inadmissible (criticised for departing from effective control); Al-Jedda v UK (2011): detention by British troops in Iraq attributable to the UK; Dutch Supreme Court, Nuhanović (2013): Dutchbat's conduct at Srebrenica attributable to the Netherlands under effective control – dual attribution possible; Mothers of Srebrenica (2019): partial liability of the Netherlands.
• UN immunity: Art 105 Charter and General Convention 1946 – national courts must respect it (Mothers of Srebrenica v Netherlands, ECtHR 2013; Haiti cholera claims in US courts); the UN must provide alternative modes of settlement (Section 29 General Convention).
Memorise: ARIO 2011 Art 7 = effective control · Behrami 2007 (UN, 'ultimate authority') vs Al-Jedda 2011 (UK) · Nuhanović 2013 (NL, dual attribution) · UN immune → Section 29 alternative.

cards.topic: International Responsibility II — Organizations, Individuals, Liability
cards.q: The International Commodity Council, an international organisation with legal personality and 30 member states, becomes insolvent and owes £900 million to private banks. The banks sue the member states. In addition, NGOs claim that the member states transferred powers to the organisation in order to evade their obligations under a human rights treaty. Are the member states responsible? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: As a rule no – an organisation with its own legal personality answers for its own acts and debts, and members are not responsible merely because of membership (International Tin Council case); but they are responsible in specific cases: aid or assistance, direction and control, coercion, circumvention of their obligations through the organisation, or acceptance of responsibility (Arts 58–62 ARIO).
• International Tin Council (J.H. Rayner v Department of Trade, House of Lords 1989): the members were not liable for the ITC's debts, which belonged to a separate legal person.
• Art 62 ARIO: a member is responsible if it has accepted responsibility or led the injured party to rely on its responsibility (presumed subsidiary).
• Art 61 ARIO – circumvention: a member that takes advantage of the organisation's competence to evade one of its own obligations, causing the organisation to commit an act that would be a breach if done by the member, is responsible (cf. ECtHR Matthews v UK 1999; Bosphorus v Ireland 2005 – presumption of equivalent protection).
• Arts 58–60 ARIO: aid or assistance, direction and control, coercion of the organisation. Conversely the organisation is responsible if its binding decisions make members commit wrongful acts (Art 17 ARIO).
Memorise: separate personality → members not liable as such (Tin Council 1989) · exceptions Arts 58–62 ARIO: aid, control, coercion, circumvention (Bosphorus), acceptance.

cards.topic: International Responsibility II — Organizations, Individuals, Liability
cards.q: Soldiers of State N (not a party to the Rome Statute), acting on the orders of N's President, kill hundreds of civilians on the territory of State P (a party) during an armed conflict. (a) Can the International Criminal Court exercise jurisdiction? (b) Does the President's official position protect him before the ICC? (c) N opens an investigation designed to shield the President. Does this bar the ICC? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes – territorial jurisdiction, since the crimes were committed on the territory of a state party (Art 12(2)(a) Rome Statute); (b) no – official capacity is irrelevant before the ICC (Art 27), although the duty of states to arrest a sitting head of a non-party state remains contested; (c) no – under complementarity a sham investigation shows unwillingness (Art 17).
• Crimes: war crimes (Art 8 – killing civilians in armed conflict), possibly crimes against humanity (Art 7 – widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population) or genocide (Art 6 – special intent); aggression (Art 8bis, active since 2018) cannot be prosecuted on a state referral or proprio motu for nationals of a non-party.
• Preconditions (Art 12): territory or nationality of a state party, or an ad hoc declaration (Art 12(3)); triggers (Art 13): state party referral, Prosecutor proprio motu (with Pre-Trial Chamber authorisation), Security Council referral under Chapter VII (Darfur 2005, Libya 2011) – the latter reaches any state.
• Individual responsibility (Art 25: ordering, aiding and abetting), superior/command responsibility (Art 28); superior orders are no defence as a rule (Art 33).
• Art 27: official capacity no ground for exemption, immunities do not bar the Court (Al-Bashir, Appeals Chamber 2019; arrest warrant against the Russian President 2023); national cooperation with arrests remains disputed (Art 98).
• Art 17: the case is admissible if the state is unwilling or unable genuinely to investigate or prosecute – unwillingness shown by proceedings to shield the person, unjustified delay, lack of independence.
Memorise: core crimes G/CAH/WC/aggression · jurisdiction = territory OR nationality of a party OR SC referral · Art 27 no immunity · Art 17 complementarity (unwilling/unable) · Art 28 command responsibility.

cards.topic: International Responsibility II — Organizations, Individuals, Liability
cards.q: Describe the development of international criminal justice from Nuremberg to the International Criminal Court, and distinguish genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. (5 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Individual criminal responsibility under international law developed from the post-war military tribunals (Nuremberg, Tokyo) through the ad hoc tribunals of the Security Council (ICTY, ICTR) and hybrid courts to the permanent ICC (Rome Statute 1998, in force 2002); the four core crimes differ in their contextual elements.
• Nuremberg IMT (London Charter 1945) and Tokyo IMTFE: crimes against peace, war crimes, crimes against humanity; crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities; Nuremberg Principles (ILC 1950): official position and superior orders no defence.
• Ad hoc tribunals created by the Security Council under Chapter VII: ICTY (Res 827 (1993), closed 2017) and ICTR (Res 955 (1994)), continued by the Residual Mechanism; hybrid courts for Sierra Leone, Lebanon, Cambodia.
• ICC: permanent, treaty-based, in The Hague, complementary to national courts.
• Genocide (Art II Genocide Convention 1948; Art 6 Rome Statute): killing, serious harm, destructive living conditions, preventing births, transferring children – with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such; no armed conflict needed.
• Crimes against humanity (Art 7): murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation, torture, rape, persecution etc. as part of a widespread or systematic attack against a civilian population pursuant to a state or organisational policy; also in peacetime.
• War crimes (Art 8): grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and serious violations of the laws of war (killing civilians or prisoners, attacks on civilian objects, prohibited weapons, pillage) – armed conflict required.
• Aggression (Art 8bis, Kampala 2010, active since 2018): planning, initiation or execution by a leader of an act of aggression that is a manifest violation of the UN Charter – a leadership crime.
Memorise: Nuremberg/Tokyo → ICTY/ICTR (SC Ch. VII) → hybrids → ICC 1998/2002 · genocide = special intent against a group · CAH = widespread/systematic attack on civilians · WC = armed conflict · aggression = leaders, manifest Charter violation.

cards.topic: International Responsibility II — Organizations, Individuals, Liability
cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? 'A soldier who follows orders cannot be punished, and his commander is liable only if he personally ordered the crimes.' Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No on both counts – superior orders are, as a rule, no defence (Nuremberg Principle IV; Art 33 Rome Statute), and commanders are liable also for failing to prevent or punish crimes of subordinates they knew or should have known about (command responsibility, Art 28).
• Art 33: an order relieves only if there was a legal obligation to obey, the person did not know it was unlawful and it was not manifestly unlawful; orders to commit genocide or crimes against humanity are always manifestly unlawful.
• Art 28: military commanders – knew or should have known and failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures to prevent, repress or report; civilian superiors – knew or consciously disregarded clear information; effective control required (Yamashita 1946; Čelebići, ICTY 1998). Official capacity is no defence either (Art 27).
Memorise: superior orders ≠ defence (Nuremberg Principle IV; Art 33 narrow exception) · command responsibility = knew/should have known + failed to prevent or punish (Art 28), civilians too.

cards.topic: International Responsibility II — Organizations, Individuals, Liability
cards.q: A satellite of the private company Orbitex (from State N) was launched by a rocket of State M from a launch site in State L at N's request. It first collides in orbit with a satellite of State R and then, on re-entry, its debris destroys a farm in State P and damages a passenger aircraft in flight over State Q. Who is liable, and on what basis? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The launching states L, M and N are jointly and severally liable – absolutely (without fault) for the damage on the surface of the earth and to the aircraft in flight (Art II Liability Convention 1972), but only for fault regarding the collision with R's satellite in orbit (Art III); no wrongful act is required.
• Liability ≠ responsibility: liability for lawful but hazardous activities, arising only where a treaty creates it.
• Launching state (Art I(c)): a state that launches or procures the launch, or from whose territory or facility an object is launched → M (launches), N (procures), L (territory) – jointly and severally liable (Art V), with recourse among themselves.
• Art II – absolute liability for damage on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight (farm in P, aircraft over Q); exoneration only for gross negligence or intent of the claimant (Art VI).
• Art III – damage elsewhere than on the earth's surface (to another space object in orbit) → liability only if due to the fault of the launching state or persons for whom it is responsible.
• Procedure: the state presents the claim through diplomatic channels (Art VIII), no exhaustion of local remedies (Art XI), Claims Commission if no settlement within a year (Art XIV). N must also authorise and supervise Orbitex (Art VI Outer Space Treaty).
• Precedent: Cosmos 954 – Soviet nuclear-powered satellite crashed in Canada 1978; settled 1981 for C$3 million.
Memorise: Liability Convention 1972: Art II absolute (earth's surface/aircraft) · Art III fault (in space) · launching state = launches/procures/territory/facility · joint and several (Art V) · Cosmos 954.

cards.topic: International Responsibility II — Organizations, Individuals, Liability
cards.q: A lawfully licensed chemical plant in State A, which complied with all regulations and every due-diligence standard, suffers an unforeseeable explosion; toxic fumes destroy crops in neighbouring State B. There is no treaty between A and B. Can B claim compensation from A under international law? Would it differ if A had authorised the plant without an environmental impact assessment and ignored repeated warnings? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: In the first scenario B has no claim against A under general international law – liability without wrongfulness exists only on the basis of a treaty (the victims may sue the operator under domestic law); in the second scenario A breached its due-diligence duty of prevention and is responsible for an internationally wrongful act.
• No-harm principle: a state must prevent significant transboundary harm from its territory (Trail Smelter 1941; Corfu Channel 1949; Nuclear Weapons AO 1996, para 29); Pulp Mills (2010): due diligence and an environmental impact assessment are required by general international law – an obligation of conduct, not of result.
• First scenario: no breach → no responsibility; liability without wrongfulness only under treaties (nuclear, oil pollution conventions). The ILC Principles on the Allocation of Loss (2006) – prompt and adequate compensation via strict operator liability, insurance, funds – are soft law.
• Second scenario: omission of A's authorities (Art 4 ARSIWA) breaching the duty of prevention → responsibility; full reparation including compensation for the crops (Arts 31, 36).
Memorise: lawful + no fault → no claim without a treaty (liability = treaty-based) · no-harm + EIA = due diligence (Trail Smelter, Pulp Mills) → breach = responsibility · ILC 2006 Principles = soft law.

cards.topic: International Responsibility II — Organizations, Individuals, Liability
cards.q: Compare state responsibility, the responsibility of international organisations and individual criminal responsibility (legal basis, nature, enforcement). Can they arise side by side from the same events? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes – all three can arise from the same events and exist in parallel: state responsibility (ARSIWA 2001, civil and compensatory, inter-state), responsibility of international organisations (ARIO 2011, modelled on it) and individual criminal responsibility (punitive, before national or international criminal courts).
• State: customary law codified in ARSIWA; attribution + breach; consequences cessation and reparation; invoked by injured or, for erga omnes obligations, other states; no criminal responsibility of states.
• International organisations: own legal personality; ARIO 2011 – attribution of organs and agents, effective control for seconded state organs (Art 7); members responsible only in special cases (Arts 58–62).
• Individuals: international law directly criminalises the core crimes (genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, aggression); enforcement by national courts (territoriality, universality) and international tribunals (ICC, ICTY, ICTR).
• Coexistence: ARSIWA is without prejudice to individual responsibility (Art 58); individual responsibility does not affect state responsibility (Art 25(4) Rome Statute). Bosnian Genocide (ICJ 2007): state responsibility for failing to prevent the Srebrenica genocide alongside ICTY convictions of individuals.
Memorise: state (ARSIWA, civil) · IO (ARIO 2011) · individual (criminal, ICC) · parallel: Art 58 ARSIWA + Art 25(4) Rome Statute · Bosnian Genocide 2007.
